This supports using endurance as an evaluation indicator, but there were few pain cases (23.4% of 47), so the estimates are imprecise.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Physical exercise improved muscle strength and pain on neck and shoulder in military pilots
authors: Wei Heng; Feilong Wei; Zhisheng Liu; Xiaodong Yan; Kailong Zhu; Fan Yang; Mingrui Du; Chengpei Zhou; Jixian Qian
what_it_does: Meta-analysis of 15 studies (907 participants) on how exercise affects neck and shoulder maximal voluntary isometric strength and pain in military pilots. Exercise increased neck flexion, extension and left and right lateral flexion strength (SMD 0.45-0.63), more so in fighter than helicopter pilots, with strength-plus-endurance rather than strength-only training, and with follow-up under 20 weeks; the overall effect on neck-pain prevalence was not significant but became significant when either of two studies was left out (OR 0.46-0.47) and was stronger in RCTs (OR 0.37), and there was no significant effect on shoulder strength or on neck and shoulder pain intensity.
why_useful: Quantifies how trainable neck strength is in military pilots by aircraft type and training mode, which informs the choice of neck-strength indicators and training-track recommendations. The evidence that exercise lowers neck-pain prevalence is weaker.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Neck Strength in Coronal and Sagittal Head Movement in Military Pilots and Aircrew With Chronic Neck Pain: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis
authors: Iã Ferreira Miranda; Edgar Santiago Wagner Neto; William Dhein; Guilherme A. Brodt; Jefferson F. Loss
venue: Journal of Manipulative and Physiological Therapeutics
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (5 studies included from 3554 search results) comparing neck strength in military pilots and aircrew with and without chronic neck pain. Flexion and extension strength did not differ, but those with neck pain had lower right (SMD -0.29, 95% CI -0.52 to -0.06) and left (SMD -0.23, 95% CI -0.45 to 0.00) lateral flexion strength.
why_useful: Points to lateral flexion (coronal-plane) neck strength, rather than flexion or extension, as the direction that is lower in aircrew with chronic neck pain, which helps choose neck-strength indicators for injury screening. The effects are small and the evidence is cross-sectional (level 3a, 5 studies).

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Pilot trainees' + 8.5 gz tolerance and fitness in their senior cadet period: a pilot study
authors: Seunghwan SHIN
venue: Gazzetta Medica Italiana Archivio per le Scienze Mediche
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Analysis of senior-cadet fitness records (3 km run, 2-min crunches and push-ups) and body composition for 108 graduates of the Korea Air Force Academy's 2018 class, grouped as passed, failed or not qualified for the +8.5 Gz (15 s) F-15 test. The 15 who qualified ran faster and did more push-ups than the 93 who did not, performance was highest in the 6 who passed, and the authors inferred 11 min 34 s for 3 km, 95 crunches and 91 push-ups as fitness levels consistent with passing.
why_useful: Links routine cadet fitness tests to high-G qualification and proposes benchmark scores, which directly informs G-tolerance indicators and cut-off-based training recommendations, though the passing group is only 6 cadets and the abstract does not explain how cadets qualified to take the test.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Changes in physical fitness and body composition of pilot cadets before and after a process of directed flight preparation
authors: Adam Prokopczyk; Zbigniew Wochyński
venue: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
what_it_does: Pre-post controlled study of 29 cadets at the Air Force Military Academy in Deblin: 17 pilot cadets completed 35 hours of directed training based on the Aviation Synthetic Efficiency Test (ASET), and 12 ground-navigation cadets followed standard physical education; fitness tests and bioimpedance body composition were measured before and after. After training the pilot cadets' fitness was at a good level while the controls' was below the standard expected for pilots; the pilot group showed larger falls in fat mass and gains in fat-free mass, muscle mass and total body water, and after training ASET correlated with body composition only in the controls.
why_useful: Shows an aviation-specific fitness test (ASET), judged against a pilot standard, used together with body composition in cadets, which informs the choice of indicators and norms and training-track recommendations; the abstract gives no ASET components or scores, and the comparison group is ground-navigation cadets rather than a randomised control.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Body Composition of Female Air Force Personnel: A Comparative Study of Aircrew, Airplane, and Helicopter Pilots
authors: Álvaro Bustamante-Sánchez; Pantelis T. Nikolaidis; Vicente Javier Clemente-Suárez
venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
what_it_does: Cross-sectional bioimpedance (InBody720) comparison of body composition in 184 female Spanish Air Force aircrew: 38 airplane pilots, 26 helicopter pilots and 120 transport aircrew. Airplane (24.0%) and helicopter (22.6%) pilots had a lower body-fat percentage than transport aircrew (26.3%), while skeletal muscle mass, soft lean mass and body water did not differ across specialties.
why_useful: Provides specialty-specific body-composition reference values for female pilots and aircrew, which informs sex-specific norms and role or aircraft-type profiles; body composition only, with no strength or performance tests.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: +Gz Exposure and Flight Duty Limitations
authors: Roope Sovelius; Tuomas Honkanen; Marjo Janhunen; Maunu Mäntylä; Heini Huhtala; Tuomo Leino
what_it_does: A survival analysis of fighter pilots who started jet training in 1995-2015 (endpoint: permanent flight-duty restriction due to spinal disorder), plus conditional logistic regression against matched controls, found an annual 0.86% spinal dropout rate and no case-control difference in sortie-by-sortie cumulative +Gz fatigue index (OR 0.96), flight hours, intensive flying periods, fitness tests or nicotine use. A maximum +Gz limitation without airframe restriction was also assessed and is presented as a useful tool for managing loading and developed symptoms.
why_useful: Fitness test results did not separate pilots who received permanent spinal flight-duty restrictions from matched controls, which is a caution for fitness-for-duty prediction models. The +Gz limitation is a concrete duty-management option, and the dropout rate gives a base rate for the outcome.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Prevalence and Potential Risk Factors for Occupational Low Back Pain Among Male Military Pilots: A Study Based on Questionnaire and Physical Function Assessment
authors: Yizhuo Yang; Shuai Liu; Mengyu Ling; Chaoqun Ye
what_it_does: Questionnaire and physical function assessment of 217 male military pilots (114 fighter, 48 helicopter, 55 transport) to identify low back pain risk factors. Weak hip external rotator strength and poor transversus abdominis activation were risk factors overall, but the significant factors differed between fighter, helicopter and transport pilots.
why_useful: Links measured hip external rotator strength and core muscle activation to low back pain in military pilots, and shows that risk factors differ by aircraft type. This can inform injury-risk indicators and weightings that vary by aircraft type.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: The effects of 12 weeks of functional strength training on muscle strength, volume and activity upon exposure to elevated Gz forces in high-performance aircraft personnel
authors: Monika Rausch; Frank Weber; Sven Kühn; Carla Ledderhos; Christoph Zinner; Billy Sperlich
what_it_does: Controlled intervention in 18 high-performance aircraft personnel (12 doing functional strength training, 6 controls), measuring isometric neck strength, MRI neck and shoulder muscle volume, and neck and back EMG in a long-arm centrifuge at +1.4 and +3 Gz with no helmet, a helmet, and a helmet with night-vision goggles. Twelve weeks of training increased maximal isometric strength and muscle volume and lowered relative muscle activation (%MVC) with a helmet under Gz, whereas perceived neck strain did not differ between groups.
why_useful: Shows that training-induced gains in isometric neck strength went with lower relative muscle activation (%MVC) under modest Gz (+1.4 and +3 Gz) while wearing a helmet. This supports neck strength as a G-related indicator and neck strength training as a recommendation for high-performance aircrew.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: An assessment of physical efficiency in cadet pilots before and after the implementation of a program preparing for flights
authors: Zbigniew Wochyński; Piotr Krawczyk; Krzysztof Cur; Zdzisław Kobos
venue: International Journal of Occupational Medicine and Environmental Health
what_it_does: Tested 35 male Polish Air Force Academy cadet pilots before and after a 70-day program on Special Aviation Gymnastic Instruments (n = 25) or standard military physical education (n = 10), using pull-ups, a 16.5-m race, a 10×10-m shuttle race, forward bends and the Aviation Synthetic Efficiency Test (ASET), with results converted into points for an overall fitness score. The training group improved significantly in pull-ups, the 16.5-m race, the shuttle race, forward bends and overall fitness, but the two groups did not differ significantly; overall fitness correlated with the component tests, including ASET.
why_useful: Offers an existing points-based composite fitness battery for cadet pilots that includes an aviation-specific test, which shows how component tests can be combined into the program's composite score. The component-to-total correlations are part-whole, and the training group did not outperform the controls.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Gz+ tolerance, body composition and ACTN-3 genotype of f-15/16 pilots
authors: Seunghwan SHIN
venue: Gazzetta Medica Italiana Archivio per le Scienze Mediche
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: In 57 Korean F-15/16 pilots, examined 9 G/15 s +Gz tolerance against ACTN-3 genotype and body composition. G tolerance was significantly related to ACTN-3 genotype (RR > RX) and, among the 40 pilots in their 30s but not the 17 in their 20s, to muscle mass and basal metabolic rate; the authors say more genes must be analysed before reliable conclusions can be drawn.
why_useful: Gives G-tolerance and body-composition (muscle mass, BMR) data in fighter pilots, with age-dependent associations, that can inform G-tolerance-related indicators; note that it measures muscle mass, not muscular strength.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Cervico-thoracic pain and associated impairments in air force personnel: a cross-sectional study
authors: Matthias Tegern; Ulrika Aasa; Helena Larsson
what_it_does: 73 Swedish air force personnel from one airbase did spinal movement-control tests, active cervical ROM and isometric cervical flexor and extensor strength and endurance tests; associations with cervico-thoracic pain (reported by 30%) were analysed with multiple binary logistic regression, and fighter pilots, helicopter pilots and rear crew were compared. Pain was associated with impaired movement control (neck flexion and forward lean tests) and reduced flexion ROM; performance was generally similar across groups, but pilots controlled the forward lean test better than rear crew, fighter pilots had greater right lateral flexion ROM than the other two groups, and fighter pilots' higher flexor strength versus rear crew was not significant.
why_useful: Compares neck movement control, ROM, strength and endurance across fighter pilots, helicopter pilots and rear crew. Performance was largely similar across roles, and strength and endurance were not among the pain-associated factors, which helps decide whether role-specific indicators are needed.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Factors associated with low back pain in air force fighter pilots: a cross-sectional study
authors: Sâmara Raquel Alves Gomes; P R F Mendes; L D O Costa; L C C Bulhões; D T Borges; Ld B Macedo; J Brasileiro
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: 28 fighter pilots were assessed for trunk muscle strength, fatigue resistance and trunk mobility, plus clinical questionnaires; 68% reported low back pain. Range of motion and trunk muscle strength did not differ between symptomatic and asymptomatic pilots, but the lateral trunk muscles fatigued sooner in pilots with low back pain.
why_useful: Points to trunk muscle fatigue resistance (endurance), rather than strength, as the measure that separated symptomatic from asymptomatic fighter pilots, though the sample is small and cross-sectional.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Muscular Fitness Improves during the First Year of Academy Studies among Fighter Pilot Cadets
authors: Tuomas Honkanen; Harri Rintala; Jani P. Vaara; Heikki Kyröläinen
venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
what_it_does: Compared maximal isometric strength (trunk flexion, trunk extension, bilateral leg extension) and muscular endurance (modified sit-up, seated dumbbell press) of 182 male fighter pilot cadets in their first Air Force Academy year and one year later. All measures increased, e.g. leg extension from 220 ± 42 to 232 ± 42 kg, trunk extension from 117 ± 21 to 120 ± 19 kg and trunk flexion from 82 ± 16 to 86 ± 17 kg.
why_useful: Supplies isometric trunk and leg strength and endurance values for fighter pilot cadets that can anchor strength indicators and reference norms for physical typing.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: The Effect of Physical Exercise Training on Neck and Shoulder Muscle Function Among Military Helicopter Pilots and Crew: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial
authors: Mike Murray; Britt Lange; Karen Søgaard; Gisela Sjøgaard
what_it_does: Secondary analysis of a randomized trial in Royal Danish Air Force helicopter pilots and crew (exercise group n = 35, reference n = 34) testing 20 weeks of self-administered neck and shoulder training on maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) and rate of torque development (RTD). Training increased cervical extension MVC (baseline 37.5 ± 11.2 Nm; p = 0.018) and RTD (p = 0.034) compared with the reference group, but only about one third of the exercise group trained regularly.
why_useful: Provides measured cervical and shoulder MVC and RTD values in helicopter aircrew for defining neck-strength indicators and reference values.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Body Composition Differences in Military Pilots and Aircrew
authors: Álvaro Bustamante-Sánchez; Vicente Javier Clemente-Suárez
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Bioimpedance study of 179 male Spanish aircrew (86 airplane pilots, 15 helicopter pilots, 78 transport aircrew). Airplane pilots had more skeletal muscle and fat-free mass and less body fat than transport aircrew, and helicopter pilots also had less body fat than transport aircrew.
why_useful: Body-composition profiles (not strength) by aircraft role that could seed role-specific physical norms. The helicopter group is small (15), and the abstract's body-fat percentage figures contradict each other (given in kg, and transport aircrew are listed at both 23.79 and 18.81), so check the numbers in the full text before citing.
notes: A submitted (pre-review) version is listed in the Universidad de la Costa repository: https://hdl.handle.net/11323/7876

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Aircrew Conditioning Programme Impact on +Gz Tolerance
authors: Ellen Slungaard; Ross D. Pollock; Alec T. Stevenson; Nicholas D. C. Green; Di J. Newham; Stephen D. R. Harridge
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser
what_it_does: Controlled study of 36 UK Royal Air Force and Royal Navy aircrew (17 performed a 12-week aerobic and muscle-strengthening Aircrew Conditioning Programme, 19 acted as controls) with centrifuge tests of relaxed and straining G tolerance and of G endurance via repeated simulated air combat manoeuvres. The programme did not change relaxed G tolerance, lowered heart rate at +5.5 Gz during straining runs, tended to improve straining G tolerance and increased the proportion completing the simulated combat profiles, with no meaningful group differences in other variables.
why_useful: Provides centrifuge-measured G-tolerance responses to strength-and-aerobic conditioning in aircrew, useful evidence for linking fitness results to training recommendations and for choosing G-related outcome measures; effects were modest and the abstract reports no strength or fitness test values.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: ACTN-3 Genotype, Body Composition, Fitness, and +Gz Tolerance in Senior Cadets
authors: Seunghwan Shin; Hyunseok Jee
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Examined ACTN-3 genotype, body composition, fitness test results (3-km run, sit-ups, push-ups), isokinetic muscle strength and endurance, and a +6 Gz 30-s G test in 68 senior Korea Air Force Academy cadets. ACTN-3 genotype (75% RR/RX, 25% XX) had no significant effect on G-test result, body composition or fitness, but body fat percentage and isokinetic peak torque (right leg extension, left leg flexion) differed significantly between G-test pass and fail groups.
why_useful: Identifies isokinetic leg strength (peak torque) and body fat percentage as candidate indicators separating G-test pass and fail in pilot candidates, relevant to strength-based suitability criteria for high-G training; the evidence is a group comparison without a predictive model, and the side-specific torque findings need confirmation.
review_trail: first rating 5 (first reviewer); second review 5; Manual review: compares G-test pass and fail groups; no prediction or classification model, so 4 rather than 5.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: NextGen Final Report: Data for Updating 14 CFR Part 25.143 and Potential Reference Standards for Part 23, 27, and 29 Aircraft: An Evaluation of Muscular Force That can be Applied to Flight Controls
authors: Dennis B. Beringer
venue: FAA Office of Aerospace Medicine technical report DOT/FAA/AM-19/5
what_it_does: FAA Civil Aerospace Medical Institute report that measured the maximum force pilots and non-pilots, sampled by age, sex and pilot status at several sites, could apply to flight controls, and compared it with the 14 CFR 25.143 reference forces as pass/fail rates and percentile distributions. Over 60% of the female samples could not reach the short-term reference force on any control, and 15-65% of the male samples failed depending on the control type.
why_useful: Gives percentile distributions of control-force strength in pilots against aircraft certification limits, the evidence base for setting strength cut-offs by aircraft category.
review_trail: first rating 5 (search agent); second review 3; No DOI; indexed in OpenAlex through the US DOT ROSA P repository. Title, author, date and the summary's figures were checked against the report PDF's own abstract. Second reviewer capped it at 3 only because the database record had no abstract; restored to 4 after the abstract was read.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: PHYSICAL FITNESS AND THE LEVEL OF LEARNING BY PILOT CADETS IN THE INITIAL PERIOD OF STUDYING IN THE POLISH AIR FORCE ACADEMY (PAFA) IN DĘBLIN
authors: Polish Air Force Academy, Dęblin, Poland; Piotr Krawczyk; Zdzisław Kobos; Cardinal Stefan Wyszynski University, Warsaw, Poland; Paweł Marcinkowski; Polish Air Force Academy, Dęblin, Poland; Robert Jędrys; Polish Air Force Academy, Dęblin, Poland; Zbigniew Wochyński; Polish Air Force Academy, Dęblin, Poland
venue: The Polish Journal of Aviation Medicine, Bioengineering and Psychology
what_it_does: Compared the physical fitness test results (pull-ups, 100 m, 1000 m and a 50 m swim) of first- and second-year pilot cadets at the Polish Air Force Academy with their semester examination averages, analysed across fitness score ranges. In both groups the fittest cadets scored above the cohort average, and the authors suggest this could support a new minimum recruitment threshold of 60 out of 100 points.
why_useful: Fitness-test data on pilot cadets (pull-ups as an upper-body strength item, plus sprint, endurance run and swim) that can inform pilot-candidate norms and a recruitment cut-off. The outcome linked to fitness is academic (semester exam) performance, not flight training, and the 60/100 threshold is a suggestion drawn from a descriptive score-range comparison, not a validated cut-off.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: G-LOC Warning Algorithms Based on EMG Features of the Gastrocnemius Muscle
authors: Sungho Kim; Taehwan Cho; Yongkyun Lee; Hyojin Koo; Booyong Choi; Dongsoo Kim
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Recorded gastrocnemius EMG from 67 Korean Air Force pilots and pilot trainees during high-G centrifuge training and examined seven EMG features, of which integrated absolute value and waveform length decayed rapidly before G-LOC. Two warning algorithms built on these features detected G-LOC with 100% sensitivity and 66.7% specificity.
why_useful: Relevant to choosing G-tolerance indicators, because calf-muscle EMG features reflecting contraction, endurance and power tracked impending G-LOC, and a pilot-specific example of sensitivity/specificity reporting, though it is a real-time warning tool rather than a fitness evaluation.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Physical fitness and aerobic capacity of Polish military fighter aircraft pilots
authors: Andrzej Tomczak; Marcin Haponik
what_it_does: Assessed 120 male Polish military fighter pilots (mean age 37.13 ± 5.42 years, split into three age groups) with a seven-item fitness test (e.g., bench push-ups 37.7 reps, pull-ups 9.1 reps, sit-ups 54 reps, standing long jump 228.5 cm) and the Åstrand-Ryhming cycle ergometer test (mean VO2max 33.73 ± 5.62 ml/kg/min). Fitness declined with age; pilots showed medium fitness and medium aerobic capacity, and aerobic capacity was lower than 30 years earlier.
why_useful: Supplies age-stratified fighter-pilot fitness test values (muscular strength-endurance, power, agility, aerobic capacity) that can serve as reference norms when setting strength-indicator thresholds for pilot typing.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Physical Condition Does Not Affect Gravity-Induced Loss of Consciousness during Human Centrifuge Training in Well-Experienced Young Aviators
authors: Jinhee Park; Chul Yun; Seungcheol Kang
what_it_does: Of 361 young male aviators with at least 2 years in high-performance aircraft, 350 with full data were split by whether they experienced G-LOC on their first human centrifuge trial (29, 8.3%) and compared on basic characteristics, body composition, physical fitness and pulmonary function. No differences in physical condition (e.g., muscle mass, strength, general endurance) were found between the G-LOC and non-G-LOC groups.
why_useful: Gives a null result from 350 experienced aviators (only 29 with G-LOC) for muscle mass, strength and endurance as determinants of G-LOC. That argues against weighting strength heavily as a G-tolerance indicator when typing pilots, though the finding may not carry over to inexperienced candidates.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Effects of the optimal flexor/extensor ratio on G-tolerance
authors: Jung Sub Park; Jean Choi; Jung Woon Kim; Sang Yun Jeon; Sunghwun Kang
what_it_does: Measured body composition and isokinetic knee and trunk strength (60°/s and 240°/s) in 77 Korea Air Force students and compared them across +6G/30 s G-tolerance test outcome groups (failed A, B, C and passed). The passing group had higher muscle mass, body fat percentage, BMI, left-knee flexion peak torque, left-knee extension work and trunk flexor/extensor ratios than one or more failing groups, and the authors conclude that balanced knee flexor/extensor ratios, a high trunk flexor/extensor ratio and, to cope with the early rapid rise in acceleration, greater maximal strength are needed.
why_useful: Directly informs the choice of strength indicators for G-tolerance-oriented typing of pilot candidates (knee and trunk flexor/extensor ratios, peak torque, body composition). Most differences were against a single failing subgroup (failed A), and the abstract does not define the failure subgroups.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: A Comparison of Cervical and Trunk Musculoskeletal Characteristics between Female and Male Army Helicopter Pilots
authors: Takashi Nagai; Karen Keenan; John Abt; Timothy Sell; Brian Smalley; Michael Wirt; Scott Lephart
venue: International Journal of Aviation, Aeronautics, and Aerospace
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser
what_it_does: Eight female Army helicopter pilots were matched 1:1 with male pilots on age and flight experience, and their cervical and trunk strength (hand-held and isokinetic dynamometry, normalised to body weight) and flexibility were compared. Female pilots had significantly lower body-weight-normalised cervical flexion, trunk flexion and trunk rotation strength, and greater cervical rotation flexibility.
why_useful: Gives pilot-specific neck and trunk strength indicators and shows sex differences that remain after body-weight normalisation, which bears on sex-specific norms or scaling for pilot types. With only 8 pairs it is preliminary and cannot supply norms on its own.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Lumbar spine and hip flexibility and trunk strength in helicopter pilots with and without low back pain history
authors: Takashi Nagai; John P. Abt; Timothy C. Sell; Karen A. Keenan; Nicholas C. Clark; Brian W. Smalley; Michael D. Wirt; Scott M. Lephart
venue: WORK: A Journal of Prevention, Assessment & Rehabilitation
what_it_does: Compared 30 helicopter pilots with a low back pain history against matched pilots without one, using isokinetic trunk and hip strength and inclinometer range of motion, including agonist/antagonist ratios and side-to-side symmetry. The LBP group had significantly lower trunk extension strength and extension/flexion strength ratio, less lateral flexion range of motion, and greater lateral flexion, rotation and hip rotation asymmetry.
why_useful: Supplies trunk-strength, strength-ratio and asymmetry indicators that distinguish helicopter pilots with an LBP history, as candidate trunk-strength indicators and injury-risk flags.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Relationships Between Physical Fitness, Demands of Flight Duty, and Musculoskeletal Symptoms Among Military Pilots
authors: Harri Rintala; Arja Häkkinen; Simo Siitonen; Heikki Kyröläinen
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: 195 male Finnish military pilots, grouped by current flight duty profile (high-G, low-G, HQ), answered a questionnaire on flying experience, flight-duty pain, resulting disability and physical activity, and the groups were compared on aerobic capacity and muscular fitness scores. The high-G group had the highest aerobic capacity and muscular fitness scores (p < 0.001), and the fittest pilots reported markedly fewer flight-duty-induced disabilities (p = 0.005) despite reporting more musculoskeletal pain.
why_useful: Informs the aircraft-type suitability and fitness-for-duty parts of the program by linking aerobic and muscular fitness to high-G duty and to flight-duty disability.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Neck Proprioception, Strength, Flexibility, and Posture in Pilots With and Without Neck Pain History
authors: Takashi Nagai; John P. Abt; Timothy C. Sell; Nicholas C. Clark; Brian W. Smalley; Michael D. Wirt; Scott M. Lephart
what_it_does: Compared 27 Army helicopter pilots with neck pain in the past 12 months against age-matched pilots without neck pain on neck proprioception, neck and scapular muscle strength, active cervical range of motion, posture and pectoralis minor length. The pain group had significantly less cervical extension and rotation range of motion, with no significant differences in strength or the other measures.
why_useful: Informs the neck-strength and injury-risk indicator set by showing which neck measures differed with neck-pain history in helicopter pilots: range of motion did, strength did not.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: 高性能歼击机飞行员体质指数与+Gz耐力分析
authors: 汪东军; 刘义欣; W.‐R. Lin; 吴建兵
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Measured height and weight (body mass index) and collected flight hours for 310 high-performance fighter pilots of different ages who passed conversion medical examinations, and related them to +Gz tolerance tested on a centrifuge (results are not given in the abstract).
why_useful: Pilot data relating body-size indices to +Gz tolerance, relevant to choosing anthropometric indicators alongside strength for fighter-aircraft suitability.
review_trail: first rating 4 (first reviewer); second review 3; Manual review of the abstract recovered from OpenAlex.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Exercise Therapy for Improved Neck Muscle Function in Helicopter Aircrew
authors: Danielle M. Salmon; Michael F. Harrison; Donald Sharpe; Darren Candow; Wayne J. Albert; J. Patrick Neary
full_text_version: the author's thesis on the same study, not the article itself
what_it_does: Randomized Canadian Forces helicopter aircrew to 12 weeks of neck coordination training (n = 10), endurance training (n = 11) or no-treatment control (n = 8), testing neck MVC strength and time to fatigue at 70% MVC in four directions. Only endurance training produced a statistically significant gain in maximal force versus control (14.4%) and coordination training improved time to fatigue in flexion and both lateral flexions, yet the abstract's conclusion reports only a positive trend and credits coordination training with the greatest strength and endurance gains.
why_useful: Supplies a neck MVC and 70%-MVC endurance test protocol used with helicopter aircrew, plus small-trial evidence on neck training options for training-track recommendations. The abstract's results and conclusion disagree on which programme improved strength most, so check the full text before citing it for a training recommendation.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Research on neck muscular strength in military pilots and the effects of muscle strength training
authors: XU Jian-hu
venue: Military Medical Journal of Southeast China
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Fifty military pilots from five aircraft groups (transport, helicopter, fighter/attack, bomber, primary trainer; 10 each) completed nine CME-1 neck training sessions over 3 weeks, with peak strength and 10-s peak impulse recorded in four directions. Transport pilots had lower flexion and extension neck strength than the other groups, and after 3 weeks peak strength had risen by 42.6% to 65.2% depending on direction.
why_useful: Gives early evidence that neck flexion and extension strength differ by aircraft type (transport pilots weaker), which bears on aircraft-type-specific neck indicators. With 10 pilots per group, no values in the abstract and a garbled significance marker, it cannot set norms on its own.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: A Predictive Logistic Regression Equation for Neck Pain in Helicopter Aircrew
authors: Michael F. Harrison; J. Patrick Neary; Wayne J. Albert; James C. Croll
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Forty helicopter aircrew provided neck-pain history, flight history and fitness results and completed isometric cervical flexion, extension and lateral-flexion MVC and time-to-fatigue (70% MVC) tests with EMG and NIRS monitoring, and logistic regression was used to identify predictors of neck pain. The final equation, built on 19 subjects, needed only the longest single NVG mission and the aircrew member's height, and cross-validation on the remaining 21 confirmed its accuracy.

Crew with neck pain trended toward lower strength (extension 55 vs 58 Nm; flexion 22 vs 24 Nm) and smaller range of motion, but no effects were statistically significant.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Evaluation of effect isotonic contraction training on neck muscles in high performance fighter pilots
authors: 高永喜; 熊万喜; 孟宪勇; 余红英; 周红; 余琳

what_it_does: Trained 98 high-performance fighter pilots on a self-designed NMT-I neck-muscle trainer (front, back, lateral and lateral-flexion pulls in six directions) and evaluated the device and training effect. Performance rose significantly after training (P<0.01; gains of 2.51-2.74 reps/min by direction), and all 37 pilots below the qualification standard beforehand met it after 4 weeks of thrice-weekly training.
why_useful: Indicator selection: supports six-direction neck strength-endurance as a fighter-pilot indicator with an existing pass standard (37 of 98 failing before training), and informs training-track recommendations.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Neck strength and myoelectric fatigue in fighter and helicopter pilots with a history of neck pain.
authors: Björn Olov Äng; Jan Linder; Karin Harms‐Ringdahl

what_it_does: Compared 16 fighter and 15 helicopter pilots who had frequent neck pain with pain-free controls on neck extensor and flexor maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) strength and on EMG fatigue during a submaximal isometric contraction. Fighter pilots with pain had lower extensor MVC than fighter controls, with no such difference for helicopter pilots or between the two control groups, while helicopter pilots with pain showed lower flexor EMG fatigue slopes than helicopter controls.
why_useful: Shows that the neck-function deficits seen with neck pain differ by aircraft type (lower extensor strength in fighter pilots, altered flexor fatigue in helicopter pilots), which supports neck screening specific to aircraft type. It does not show a strength difference between pain-free fighter and helicopter pilots.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Neck muscle strength and endurance in fighter pilots: effects of a supervised training program.

what_it_does: Two groups of 20 fighter pilots at different bases did the same neck exercise programme for 6-8 months, one with weekly physical-therapist reinforcement and one unsupervised, with isometric neck flexor and extensor strength and endurance measured before and after. The reinforced group gained strength (flexors 3.9 Nm, extensors 5.0 Nm) and extensor endurance (53 s), the unsupervised group lost extensor strength (11.5 Nm) and endurance (33 s), and neck complaints did not change in either group.
why_useful: Supplies isometric neck flexor and extensor strength and extensor endurance measures in fighter pilots. It also gives non-randomized evidence that physiotherapist-reinforced training went with gains while unsupervised training did not, which can inform training recommendations.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Acceleration effects on neck muscle strength: pilots vs. non-pilots.

what_it_does: Single-day cross-sectional comparison of maximal isometric neck strength in 10 fighter pilots and 10 non-pilots, measured in extension, flexion and left and right lateral bending on a computerized dynamometer. Pilots' overall neck strength did not differ from non-pilots' and no direction-specific strength changes attributable to +Gz exposure were found, so the authors recommend on-ground neck strengthening plus in-flight head positioning to minimise +Gz-induced neck injury.
why_useful: Provides a four-direction dynamometer protocol for neck strength in fighter pilots and supports having the program assess and train neck strength rather than assume flying builds it; n=10 per group and the abstract reports no strength values.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Anti-G effect of coordinated muscle straining training in high performance fighter pilots and Jian-fighter pilots
authors: LUO Min; 李诗伟; Wang Hong
venue: 中华航空航天医学杂志

what_it_does: Evaluated coordinated muscle-straining anti-G training in 44 high-performance fighter pilots (initial course plus two refresher courses) and 99 Jian-fighter pilots (initial course), measuring thigh and calf static muscle force, hold time and SBP during the manoeuvre and estimating +Gz tolerance. Static force and hold time rose after training (P<0.05), the standardized manoeuvre raised SBP over baseline by 51.8 and 46.0 mmHg (estimated +2.8 and +2.6 G), and failure rates were 27.27% (high-performance, refresher) vs 48.48% (Jian, initial).
why_useful: Provides fighter-pilot data on lower-limb static force during the anti-G straining manoeuvre, SBP-based estimates of +Gz tolerance gain, and a training pass standard with failure rates. These could inform G-related indicators and training recommendations. The abstract does not relate muscle force to G tolerance, and the failure-rate gap between the two pilot groups is confounded with refresher versus initial training.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: The effect of aircraft control forces on pilot performance during instrument landings in a flight simulator.
authors: David J Hewson; Peter John McNair; Bob Marshall
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Twelve pilots flew five simulated instrument landings with control forces set relative to each pilot's maximal aileron-right force (90%, 60%, 30%), at normal force and at 25% of normal, while EMG, control forces and glide-slope deviation were recorded. Landing accuracy was worst at 90% of maximal force, which the authors attribute to greater force variability, and they conclude designers must consider pilot strength limits when specifying new standards.
why_useful: Simulator evidence from pilots that landing accuracy drops when control forces near each pilot's maximal strength. This supports using relative-strength margins, not only absolute minimum strength, as indicators for aircraft-type suitability, though the sample is only 12 pilots.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands

Pilots had higher flexor and extensor strength (47 and 65 Nm vs 36 and 59 Nm), which the authors suggest may reflect work-related muscle strain and/or differences in muscle fiber composition that might be reflected by pilot selection procedures.
why_useful: Reference neck-strength values for jet pilots versus non-pilots that could anchor pilot-specific strength norms. The two groups differ in age, which limits the comparison.

title: Aircraft control forces and EMG activity in a C-130 Hercules during strength-critical maneuvers.

Forces were similar to aircraft design standards, but left rudder pedal force and vastus lateralis activity were greater in the engine-off maneuvers, and the vastus lateralis activation seen there could be sustained for only about 1 min.
why_useful: Adds rudder and leg force and muscle-endurance demands for a transport aircraft, for aircraft-type strength criteria. It shows that sustained endurance, not only peak force, can limit performance. Based on six subjects only.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Aircraft control forces and EMG activity in a UH-1H Iroquois helicopter during emergency maneuvers.

Cyclic and collective forces consistently exceeded military design standards, yet muscle activity stayed sub-maximal and all pilots completed the maneuvers.
why_useful: Helicopter-specific control-force and muscle-activation data for setting aircraft-type strength requirements. The authors caution that comparing pilot strength with design standards may overestimate how many pilots can produce the forces needed. Based on six pilots only.

In linear regression, aerobic power explained 9% of the variance in the selection performance score and anaerobic power an additional 3%.
why_useful: Gives empirical effect sizes linking aerobic and anaerobic fitness to pilot-candidate selection scores (and body fat to acceptance), useful when weighting physical scores in a selection recommendation; no muscular-strength measure was included.

The data helped develop standards for evaluating pilots' physical work capacity and were compared with published norms, including US Air Force working norms.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Determinants of +Gz-related neck pain: a preliminary survey.

Frequency of muscle endurance training was the only possible determinant.
why_useful: An early test in student pilots of measured strength indicators (grip and isometric neck strength) against an in-flight pain outcome. The strength measures did not emerge as determinants, which matters when choosing indicators, though the study is small and preliminary.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Unpredictability of fighter pilot G tolerance using anthropometric and physiologic variables.
authors: James T. Webb; C J Oakley; Larry J. Meeker

what_it_does: Correlation and multiple regression analyses related the centrifuge G tolerance of 1,434 fighter pilots in High-G Training to anthropometric and physiologic variables; a four-variable model (relaxed gradual-onset G tolerance inversely related to height and directly related to age, weight and diastolic blood pressure) explained more variation than any single variable, but no correlation exceeded r = 0.35. No variable differed between pilots who did and did not have G-induced loss of consciousness, and the authors conclude that this kind of prediction is unreliable and that the anti-G straining maneuver is the major determinant of G tolerance.
why_useful: A large-sample negative result: anthropometric and physiologic variables predicted pilot G tolerance poorly (the abstract mentions no strength measures). Any body- or strength-based typing that claims to predict G tolerance should be compared against this baseline.

title: Isometric abdominal muscle training and G tolerance.

Training did not change G tolerance, maximal IAP or knee-extensor peak torque (leg muscle endurance rose and perceived exertion fell), but static knee-extensor endurance correlated positively with G tolerance (p<0.05).
why_useful: Helps choose indicators for high-G aircraft suitability: links a specific muscular measure (static knee-extensor endurance) to centrifuge G tolerance in fighter pilots, though the correlation rests on 10 pilots and the abdominal training itself did not raise G tolerance.

title: Effects of strength training on G tolerance.

ACM time rose by 39%, knee-extensor strength in slow contractions by 17% and anaerobic power by 14%, while aerobic performance and vastus lateralis histochemistry were unchanged.
why_useful: Pre-post evidence that strength training, with knee-extensor strength gains, was followed by longer centrifuge ACM tolerance in fighter pilots; supports treating muscular strength as relevant to high-G suitability and to strength-training recommendations, though n=11 and no control group is mentioned in the abstract.

Weak men and weak women had similar leg strength, strong women's arm strength matched weak men's, training improved leg strength more than arm strength, and most women and some men fell below the control-resistance specification for current aircraft.

title: Human limits in next-generation fighter aviation: psychophysiological stressors, readiness, health, performance, and countermeasures
authors: Jennifer F. Chan; Jing Zhang; Maria Y. Shiu; Fethi Bouak; Kaela Shea; Joan Saary; Oshin Vartanian; Shawn G. Rhind
what_it_does: Narrative review of psychophysiological demands in fifth- and sixth-generation fighter aviation (sustained high-G, hypoxia/hyperoxia, cognitive load, sensory, thermal and musculoskeletal stress), finding measurable but highly individualized responses and limited direct fifth-generation evidence. Proposes a staged readiness-monitoring framework combining cardiovascular-autonomic, neurocognitive, sensory, wearable and biomarker data, with AI/ML treated as an experimental layer needing prospective validation and human aeromedical oversight retained.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: The effects of different neck training methods on the neck function of aviation cadets
authors: Hao Luo; Dingyu Zhao; Xueru Jia
what_it_does: Compared 12 weeks of helmet-style neck training, elastic-band neck training and regular resistance training with no added neck work (control) in aviation cadets, testing neck strength in six directions and neck endurance at baseline, 6 and 12 weeks. Both neck-training groups gained strength in all six directions at 6 and 12 weeks (significant time-by-group interactions); all groups improved endurance by 6 weeks, the elastic-band and control groups did not change after that, and the helmet group had significantly higher endurance at 12 weeks (103.55 ± 47.68 s).
why_useful: Trainability evidence: shows that six-direction neck strength and neck endurance in pilot candidates respond to 12 weeks of targeted neck training, with helmet-style training better for endurance. This can inform neck-training recommendations. The abstract gives no sample size and no baseline values that could serve as norms.

It covers breath-hold training, muscle strength and endurance training, aerobic versus anaerobic training and combined physical-cognitive training, notes that lower-body and trunk isometric force during AGSM falls with fatigue, and says the evidence on strength, endurance, aerobic and anaerobic training is contradictory.
why_useful: Background for choosing indicators: it summarises which strength, endurance and aerobic qualities may support +Gz tolerance and where the evidence conflicts.

Preflight lower-body strength accounted for 20-40% of the variability in selected functional performance outcomes, and in-flight cycle and treadmill exercise volumes were associated with aerobic fitness.
why_useful: Evidence for choosing indicators: shows how strength and aerobic measures relate to operational task performance in an aerospace crew population.

Of 38 fitness metrics identified, 8 cardiovascular and 12 muscular metrics were associated with simulated EVA task performance.

It outlines field assessment protocols (handheld dynamometry, endurance-hold benchmarks) and programming for the neck, trunk and lower limbs, and calls for normative and dose-response data.

title: Glycated Hemoglobin vs. Fasting Glucose in Routine Screening of Military Aircrew

what_it_does: Compared fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c screening in 175 male Polish Air Force pilots aged 45-60 at periodic medical examinations, and used multivariate regression to relate age, BMI and body fat percentage to glycemic status. FPG classed more pilots as prediabetic than HbA1c did (53.1% vs 30.3%), and body fat percentage was more strongly associated with HbA1c than age or BMI.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Individualized Cardiovascular Modeling for Operationally Relevant Altered-Gravity Scenarios
authors: Hrudayavani S. Vellore; Madison Herrmann; Cort Reinarz; Amanda E. Kraft; Raquel C. Galvan-Garza; Nancy Currie-Gangg; Ana Diaz-Artiles
what_it_does: Simulation study that uses a 21-compartment lumped-parameter cardiovascular model of seated individuals in G Warm Up and parabolic-flight scenarios to estimate how sex, height, body mass, blood volume, body surface area, athletic ability and hydration affect heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output and blood pressure. Differences between individuals grew with gravity level: larger individuals showed lower heart rate and higher stroke volume, cardiac output and blood pressure; dehydration raised heart rate and lowered cardiac output and blood pressure; athleticism lowered heart rate (especially in men), while athletic females showed lower stroke volume than non-athletic females.
why_useful: Points to body size, fitness and hydration factors that change G-related cardiovascular responses, which can guide the choice of indicators for the program's G-tolerance component, though the evidence comes from simulation rather than measured pilots.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Lower-Limb Neuromuscular Profiles from Force Plate Testing During Elite Women’s Basketball National Team Camps: A Retrospective Comparison by Final Roster Status
authors: Hiroki Ogata; Kazuya Yamazaki; Tomohiro Usui; Kotaro Shinchi; Katsuya Ikeda; Frederick James Henderson; Daichi Yamashita

After adjusting for age and playing position, no between-group differences were found (all p >= 0.12); roster players were older and more internationally experienced, suggesting selection reflected factors beyond these tests.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Analysis of physical fitness tests for police officers in various countries: a scoping review
authors: Zhaohua Zhang; Jian He; Xiaohui Zhang; Liru Zhao; Yujian Deng
what_it_does: Scoping review of Chinese and English databases up to December 2024 that analysed 16 police physical fitness tests from 7 countries and grouped them into basic fitness-item batteries (n=9) and job-simulation obstacle courses (n=7). Cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength and endurance, and agility were the most used components; the authors conclude that no single model is optimal and that test design should rest on selection efficiency, ecological validity and cultural applicability.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Fitness profile and training of Special Operation Forces: a comparison with sports athletes
authors: Alain Dössegger; Thomas Gsponer; Martin Flück; Christian Protte; Thomas Wyss; Eric Häusler; Markus Gerber; Oliver Faude

what_it_does: In 262 men (69 Swiss Special Operations Forces operators, 175 candidates, 18 sports athletes), practitioner interviews defined mission-critical success factors that were turned into a test battery of reaction time, power, strength, work capacity and aerobic endurance, and groups were compared with Bayesian linear regression. Operators and candidates showed fitness comparable to athletes (reported means included relative hand-grip strength 1.51 kg/kg and VO2max 54 ml/kg/min), though both did fewer 100 kg deadlift repetitions than athletes, and the authors present the norms and battery as a tool for selection and readiness assessment.

title: Normative values for the Measure of strength and Body composition in Athletes: A cross-sectional Study
authors: Zahi Gergi Andraos
venue: International Journal of Kinesiology and Sports Science
what_it_does: Cross-sectional study of 264 Lebanese adults aged 18-40 (162 men, 102 women), grouped as resistance-trained or untrained, measuring handgrip maximal force, rate of force development and body composition, with groups compared by MANOVA and graded with a seven-class normative system. Trained participants, particularly women, showed higher strength and better body composition, and normative bands from 'Very Poor' to 'Superior' were set for handgrip and explosive strength.
why_useful: A template for norm-referenced grading of handgrip maximal force and rate of force development that the program could rebuild on pilot data to define strength-level categories.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Efficacy of Core Muscle Exercise Combined with Interferential Therapy in Alleviating Chronic Low Back Pain in High-Performance Fighter Pilots: A Randomized Controlled Trial
authors: Chongwen Zuo; Zhiyang Zheng; Xiaoyan Ma; Fen Wei; Yushui Wang; Yi Yin; Shuai Liu; Xiaosong Cui; Chaoqun Ye
what_it_does: Randomised 53 Chinese Air Force fighter pilots with chronic low back pain to 12 weeks of core-muscle exercise plus interferential current, exercise alone, or interferential current alone, with trunk muscle strength, endurance and range of motion as secondary outcomes. All groups improved; combined therapy reduced pain more than either monotherapy, and core muscle function gains were similar for combined therapy and exercise alone.
why_useful: Shows trunk strength and endurance as trainable indicators linked to back pain in fighter pilots, which informs indicator selection and training-track recommendations for pilots with back pain.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Reliability of a Flight Helmet-Attached Force Gauge in Measuring Isometric Neck Muscle Strength
authors: Tuomas Honkanen; Ville Mattila; Otto Kinnunen; Marjo Janhunen; Roope Sovelius; Jani P. Vaara; Heikki Kyröläinen
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Tested intra- and interrater reliability of a commercial force gauge attached to a flight helmet for maximal isometric neck flexion, extension and lateral flexion in 41 subjects (31 for interrater testing). Interrater reliability was good (ICC 0.79-0.90) and intrarater moderate to good (ICC 0.58-0.84); flexion was consistently good (ICC 0.84-0.89), lateral flexion moderate to good (0.73-0.90) and extension lowest (intrarater 0.58, interrater 0.79).
why_useful: Choice of measurement: a helmet-mounted isometric neck-strength test that the authors judge reliable, safe and clinically applicable for flexion and lateral flexion but weaker for extension. This tells the program which neck indicators can be measured dependably. The abstract does not say the subjects were pilots.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Impact of a 12-wk physical conditioning program on the aerobic capacity of aviation cadets
authors: Hao Luo; Ding-Yu Zhao; Juan Li
what_it_does: Randomised 55 aviation cadets to a 12-week anti-G fitness programme (strength training twice and HIIT three times weekly, plus nutritional and psychological support) or usual training, measuring VO2max, lower-limb strength and haemoglobin. VO2max showed no significant group-by-time interaction, though paired tests favoured the training group, and lower-limb strength and haemoglobin differed over time and between groups.
why_useful: Informs what to put in an anti-G conditioning track for pilot candidates and which outcomes to track (VO2max, lower-limb strength).

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Force-velocity-power variables derived from isometric and dynamic testing: metrics reliability and the relationship with jump performance
authors: Amilton Vieira; Rafael Cunha; Carlos Gonçalves; Juliano Dal Pupo; James Tufano
what_it_does: In 15 male combat-sports athletes, force-velocity-power variables and the dynamic strength index were derived from isometric mid-thigh pull and squat-jump testing, and the study assessed their within-session reliability and their correlations with jump height and impulse. All variables showed acceptable reliability (ICC moderate to excellent, mean CV <10%). Theoretical maximal power correlated very largely with jump impulse, while jump height correlated with none of the variables.
why_useful: Supports using force-velocity-power and DSI metrics from the IMTP and squat jump as reliable muscular-strength indicators for the strength-typing component, though the sample is small.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: The dynamic strength index is a reliable and feasible tool to assess neuromuscular performance in male and female handball players
authors: Carlos García-Sánchez; Jose María Lominchar-Ramos; Ester Jiménez-Ormeño; Paul Comfort; Diego A. Alonso-Aubín; Marcos A. Soriano
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: In 35 semi-professional handball players (17 male, 18 female), the study measured force-plate test-retest reliability of isometric mid-thigh pull metrics and the dynamic strength index (using countermovement-jump peak propulsive force) with ICC, CV, SEM and smallest detectable difference. Reliability was good to excellent (ICC 0.78-0.97, CV <=8.64%), although peak propulsive force (all players) and DSI (females) differed significantly between sessions.
why_useful: Its reliability statistics (ICC, CV, SEM, smallest detectable difference) for IMTP and DSI can set measurement-error thresholds for the strength indicators used in pilot typing.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: A Flight Helmet-Attached Force Gauge for Measuring Isometric Neck Muscle Strength
authors: Paavo Nyländen; Mikko Virmavirta; Roope Sovelius; Heikki Kyröläinen; Tuomas Honkanen
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Compared a force gauge attached to a flight helmet against a weight-stack machine for maximal isometric neck flexion, extension and lateral flexion in 10 subjects, recording EMG of the neck muscles. Mean forces differed significantly between devices in all directions but correlated at r = 0.73-0.89, and the authors judged the gauge valid for comparing individuals and tracking strength change.
why_useful: Supporting validity evidence for a pilot-specific neck-strength test when choosing measurement tools, with the caveat that its absolute forces cannot be swapped for machine-based values.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Association of Genotype, High-G Tolerance, and Body Composition in Jet Aircraft Aviators
authors: Seunghwan Shin
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Genotyped ACTN3 and ACE in 81 Korean F-15/F-16 pilots who underwent +8.5 Gz centrifuge testing and related genotype to high-G tolerance (mean breathing interval) and body composition. The ACTN3 RR genotype was significantly associated with +8.5 Gz tolerance and ACE showed a trend (P = .057), while body composition was unrelated to genotype; the authors call the study preliminary.
why_useful: Gives G-tolerance data on fighter pilots and names genotype as a possible fixed covariate of G-tolerance, relevant to background on what drives G-tolerance and to fairness review.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Comparing Body Composition Methods for Air Force Reserve Officers’ Training Corps Cadets
authors: Trey R Naylor; Jessica E Kiss; Adam M Fullenkamp; David K Garon

what_it_does: Compared air displacement plethysmography, bioelectrical impedance, skinfolds and the Air Force circumference method, plus BMI-based compliance, in 24 Air Force ROTC cadets (21 men, 3 women) using repeated-measures ANOVA. Only skinfolds and bioelectrical impedance differed significantly, and BMI classed more cadets as non-compliant (7) than circumferences did (1).
why_useful: Informs the choice of body-composition measurement and cautions against using BMI alone for compliance or classification decisions.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Assessment of the psychomotor fitness level of cadet pilots after a 6-month flight training period - pilot study
authors: Zbigniew Wochyński; Justyna Skrzyńska-Rękawek; Zdzisław Kobos
what_it_does: Tested 20 male Polish Air Force Academy cadet pilots before and after 6 months of flight training on a physical-effort test (rotations on a looping apparatus) with cognitive tasks delivered through wireless glasses, plus heart rate and blood pressure. Task completion improved significantly and post-effort systolic pressure fell, but the gain in looping rotations was not significant.
why_useful: Describes a pilot-specific dual-task psychomotor fitness test that could be considered as an aviation-specific indicator, though the evidence is weak.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Influence of Body Composition, Load-Velocity Profiles, and Sex-Related Differences on Army Combat Fitness Test Performance
authors: David Boffey; Joseph A. DiPrima; Kristina L. Kendall; Ethan C. Hill; Jeffrey R. Stout; David H. Fukuda
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: In 72 Army ROTC cadets (55 men, 17 women) tested at two time points four months apart, stepwise regression showed muscle mass and body-fat percentage explained 49% of shared variance in total Army Combat Fitness Test score, and hex-bar deadlift load-velocity maximal power and velocity explained 67%. Men outperformed women on every event, most on the standing power throw and sprint-drag-carry.
why_useful: Informs indicator selection and sex-specific norms by showing which strength-power (load-velocity) and body-composition measures account for a composite military fitness test score.
notes: The first author's 2021 doctoral dissertation on the same study is free at https://stars.library.ucf.edu/etd2020/650/

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Core stabilisation exercises reduce chronic low back pain in Air Force fighter pilots: a randomised controlled trial
authors: Priscilla Rique Furtado Mendes; S R A Gomes; L D O Costa; A D A L Liguori; L C C Bulhões; J S Brasileiro
full_text_version: the author's thesis on the same study, not the article itself
what_it_does: Randomised controlled trial in 14 Brazilian Air Force fighter pilots with chronic low back pain, comparing a 12-week, twice-weekly core stabilisation programme (n=7) with their usual exercise routine (n=7). The stabilisation group had larger reductions in low back pain (2.3 points) and cervical pain (2.5 points) and kept its trunk strength, while the usual-exercise group lost right-side flexion strength (between-group difference -3.7%); disability, range of motion and fatigue resistance did not differ.
why_useful: Informs the training-recommendation side of decision support (core stabilisation for pilots with low back pain) and supports isometric trunk strength as a pilot indicator, within the limits of a 14-pilot trial.
notes: The saved PDF is the first author's 2022 doctoral thesis, in Portuguese; its Study I (from page 7 of the thesis) reports this trial.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Effects of Cardiovascular Disease Risk Factors, Musculoskeletal Health, and Physical Fitness on Occupational Performance in Firefighters—A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Jaron Ras; Andre P. Kengne; Denise L. Smith; Elpidoforos S. Soteriades; Rucia V. November; Lloyd Leach
venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
what_it_does: Systematic review and meta-analysis relating cardiovascular risk factors, musculoskeletal health and physical fitness to firefighters' occupational task performance. Cardiorespiratory fitness (R = -0.584), grip strength (R = -0.421), upper-body strength (R = -0.318), lower-body strength (R = -0.216), and upper-body and abdominal endurance were significantly correlated with occupational performance (negative coefficients as reported), and older firefighters with poorer body composition and lower fitness performed worse on all tasks.
why_useful: Gives meta-analytic effect sizes linking strength and fitness tests to job-task performance in a tactical population, which helps in choosing and weighting job-relevant strength indicators.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands

full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Practitioner article presenting a needs analysis of the static and dynamic physical demands of US Air Force Special Operations Command aircrew positions, to inform the design of strength and conditioning programmes. It proposes a testing protocol for obtaining objective measures to guide training design and progression; the abstract reports no collected data.
why_useful: Offers a demands analysis and candidate test battery specific to aircrew, which can guide which strength and fitness indicators the program measures for different crew positions.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Atherogenic Risk, Anthropometry, Diet and Physical Activity in a Sample of Spanish Commercial Airline Pilots
authors: Ana Alaminos-Torres; Jesús Román Martínez-Álvarez; Noemi López-Ejeda; Maria Dolores Marrodán-Serrano
venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
what_it_does: Cross-sectional study of 304 male Spanish commercial airline pilots that used clinical history, anthropometry, bioelectrical impedance, and diet and physical-activity questionnaires to relate their profiles to the atherogenic index of plasma (AIP). 53.6% had excess weight and 64.6% abdominal obesity; AIP rose with obesity indicators and LDL cholesterol and was inversely related to Mediterranean-diet adherence and vigorous physical activity.
why_useful: Gives pilot-specific body-composition and cardiometabolic-risk data that could inform body-composition indicators and reference values in the health-related part of the comprehensive evaluation.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Relationship between a Maximum Plank Assessment and Fitness, Health Behaviors, and Moods in Tactical Athletes: An Exploratory Study
authors: Megan Sax van der Weyden; Michael Toczko; Marcie Fyock-Martin; Joel Martin
venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
what_it_does: Exploratory study of 49 tactical athletes that correlated maximum plank hold time (an Army Combat Fitness Test event) with fitness tests and with lifestyle and mood surveys, and compared those who passed and failed the plank. Plank time correlated with body mass, fat mass, BMI, push-ups and state physical energy; VO2max differed between the pass and fail groups, while lifestyle behaviours and trait moods were not associated.
why_useful: Informs the choice and interpretation of a trunk-endurance indicator (the plank) in the fitness test battery, given its links to body composition, aerobic fitness and day-to-day state.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: The Effects of Body Composition, Physical Fitness on Time of Useful Consciousness in Hypobaric Hypoxia
authors: Keunsoo Kim; Jean Choi; On Lee; Jungjun Lim; Jungwoon Kim
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Participants had body composition and fitness tests, then hypobaric hypoxia exposure at a simulated 25,000 ft, and time of useful consciousness (TUC) was modelled with correlation and multiple regression. TUC correlated positively with VO2max and sit-up and push-up endurance and negatively with body fat, and the regression explained 84.5% of TUC; the abstract does not describe the participant population.
why_useful: A regression linking cardiorespiratory, muscular-endurance and body-composition indicators to an aviation-specific tolerance outcome, so a possible extra criterion. The 84.5% figure is in-sample, and the population and sample size need checking in the full text.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Associations between ACE Genotypes, +8.5 Gz Tolerance, and Body Composition in F-15 Pilot Candidates
authors: Seunghwan Shin; Seokhee Son
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: In 20 Korean F-15 pilot candidates, related ACE genotype to passing a 15-s +8.5 Gz test and to body composition. Half passed, with pass rates of 75% (DD), 66.7% (DI) and 30% (II) (P < .05, DD > II), and the DD genotype was associated with higher body composition values, more prominently among those who passed; the authors say the results need further investigation.
why_useful: Background for aircraft-type (F-15) G suitability: gives +8.5 Gz pass/fail data and a genotype-linked body-composition pattern in pilot candidates, but the grouping is genetic rather than strength-based, body-composition values are not given in the abstract and n=20.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: [Research on the influence of 12-week basic load resistance training on the physical fitness of flight students in an aviation school].
authors: Zhe Ji; Hai-Tao Zhou; Zhi-Kang Zou; Xian Guo; Xin Zhang; Hui Cao; Zhi‐Dong Jiang; Xiang Ren; Anli Wang; Jian-Min Cao

what_it_does: Randomized 37 male flight students at an aviation school to 12 weeks of anti-G-oriented training (HIIT plus high-intensity strength training, n=18) or control (n=19). The training group significantly increased lean and muscle mass, lower-limb push strength, trunk isometric strength, and physical-activity energy expenditure and step counts versus control.
why_useful: Shows which strength qualities (lower-limb push and trunk isometric strength) are treated as key anti-G indicators in pilot students and that they respond to training, informing strength-indicator selection.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Comparison of Different Variants of the U.S. Army Occupational Physical Assessment Test
authors: Barry A Spiering; Kathryn M Taylor; Bruce S Cohen; Nathaniel I Smith; David J Zeppetelli; Vincent P Pecorelli; P Matthew Bartlett; Leila A Walker; Peter N Frykman; Stephen A Foulis
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: 32 participants (14 men, 18 women) aged 18-42 did, in random order, two versions each of the U.S. Army OPAT seated power throw (from the ground vs from a chair) and strength deadlift (hex bar vs paired dumbbells). The chair throw (5.4 vs 5.0 m) and hex-bar deadlift (86.9 vs 83.1 kg) gave significantly higher scores, though the two versions of each test were strongly correlated (tau 0.90 and 0.83).
why_useful: Informs how strength measurement is standardised: changes in equipment and posture shift scores in a strength-based job-placement test, so protocols must be fixed before norms or cut-offs are set.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Cross-sectional area of the paraspinal muscles and its association with muscle strength among fighter pilots: a 5-year follow-up
authors: Tuomas Honkanen; Matti Mäntysaari; Tuomo Leino; Janne Avela; Liisa Kerttula; Ville Haapamäki; Heikki Kyröläinen
what_it_does: Followed 26 Finnish Air Force male fighter pilots with lumbar MRI at baseline and after 5 years, with maximal isometric strength tested once at baseline. Paraspinal muscle cross-sectional area (CSA) rose by 8% at L3-4 and 7% at L4-5, paraspinal and psoas CSA were positively related to baseline overall isometric strength, and neither CSA nor muscle composition was associated with low back pain.
why_useful: Background on trunk-muscle size in young fighter pilots: paraspinal and psoas CSA was related to overall isometric strength, and CSA was not linked to low back pain, which argues against using muscle size as a low-back-pain risk marker. The abstract reports no strength values.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Effect of different combat jet manoeuvres in the psychophysiological response of professional pilots
authors: Alberto J. Hormeño-Holgado; Vicente J. Clemente-Suárez
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Measured 29 fighter pilots before and after offensive and defensive combat manoeuvres on heart rate and HRV, leg and hand strength, spirometry, lactate, hydration, cortical activation, memory and psychological variables. The defensive manoeuvre lowered forced vital capacity and increased leg strength, and both manoeuvres raised mean heart rate, perceived stress and perceived exertion.
why_useful: Describes the acute physical load of air-combat manoeuvres, including strength changes, which can help justify which strength and cardiorespiratory indicators the program targets.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Fitness Profiles in Elite Tactical Units: A Critical Review
authors: Daniel Maupin; Thomas Wills; Robin M. Orr; Benjamin Schram
what_it_does: Critical review of 14 studies on the fitness profiles of elite tactical units, appraised with the Downs and Black checklist (quality 46% to 66%, mean 57.5%). Anthropometry, strength, power and aerobic capacity were the most common domains, but measures and protocols varied widely and no standardized measure or result exists for this population.
why_useful: Helps choose and standardise the anthropometric, strength, power and aerobic indicator domains of a military fitness battery, and flags evidence-quality gaps the program should avoid.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Impact of exercise programs among helicopter pilots with transient LBP
authors: Knut Andersen; Roald Baardsen; Ingvild Dalen; Jan Petter Larsen
what_it_does: Thirty-nine helicopter pilots (35 men, 4 women) with flight-related low back pain were allocated to either a 10-exercise general LBP programme or a 4-exercise lumbar trunk endurance programme for 3 months, with questionnaires, trunk muscular endurance tests and ultrasound of lumbar multifidus contractility before and after. About half trained per protocol; overall, muscle endurance, multifidus contractility, function and quality of health improved, and the endurance-specific programme significantly improved pain, function and quality of health.
why_useful: Informs the training-recommendation side of decision support by supporting trunk muscular endurance as a trainable indicator and an exercise track for helicopter pilots with flight-related LBP.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: The role of physical training on G-force tolerance in fighter pilots
authors: Patrícia de Castro de Paiva

what_it_does: Narrative book chapter describing a fighter-pilot physical training programme (strength, muscular endurance, aerobic, stretching and neck exercises) and summarising evidence that gains in strength and muscular endurance appear to increase G-force tolerance. It notes that some centrifuge findings on strength and +Gz tolerance were statistically nonsignificant, and that high aerobic conditioning decreases orthostatic tolerance.
why_useful: Gives background reasons for which strength and endurance components to weight, and which not to overweight, when linking pilot strength profiles to G-tolerance suitability and training tracks.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: The prevalence of overweight and obesity vs. the level of physical activity of aviation military academy students
authors: Agata Gaździńska; Paulina Baran; Franciszek Skibniewski; Olaf Truszczyński; Stefan Gaździński; Mariusz Wyleżoł
what_it_does: Assessed BMI, body fat and accelerometer-measured physical activity in 100 cadets of the Polish Air Force Military Academy in Dęblin. By BMI, 25.3% were overweight and 3.4% obese; normal BMI fell from 88% of 1st-2nd-year to 48.6% of 4th-5th-year cadets, and daily distance covered was lower in senior years.
why_useful: Provides body-composition and activity reference data for aviation cadets, relevant to anthropometric indicators, norms and tracking change across training years.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Effect of Targeted Strength, Endurance, and Coordination Exercise on Neck and Shoulder Pain Among Fighter Pilots
authors: Britt Lange; Palle Toft; Corrie Myburgh; Gisela Sjøgaard

what_it_does: Randomized 55 Danish F-16 pilots to 24 weeks of targeted neck strength, endurance and coordination training (n = 27) or no-treatment control (n = 28), with a baseline clinical examination including the craniocervical flexion test. 82% reported neck pain in the past year, and training reduced 3-month neck pain from 2.0 to 1.0 versus control (P = 0.01).
why_useful: Informs training recommendations for fighter pilots with neck pain and offers the craniocervical flexion test as a candidate neck-function measure.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Effect of neck muscular strength training at different time durations for military pilots

what_it_does: Trained 60 military pilots for 2 or 3 weeks (and 11 'military smithery' personnel for 6 weeks) on the CME-1 neck training device, measuring neck strength and 10-s peak impulse in flexion, extension and both lateral flexions in isometric and variable velocity-resistance modes. Pilots' neck strength reportedly improved significantly, with average strength in the four directions rising by 47.3%, 44.8%, 70.5% and 59.6% after 3 weeks.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: The reasons of fighter aircraft high +Gz induced pilot's neck injuries and prevention
authors: Lüe Deng; Jin Zhao; Xi-chen Geng; Lihui Zhang; Hong Wang; Haixia Wang; Yifeng Li; Quan Wang
