what_it_does: Narrative review of 50 published papers on why high +Gz exposure in fighter aircraft injures pilots' necks, listing consensus risk factors (+Gz threshold, head load, passive effects in the back seat, unsuitable head posture, frequent high +Gz exposure). Prevention centres on cervical spine function evaluation, neck muscle strength training, protective equipment and better man-machine fit, and the authors call for integrated prevention.
why_useful: Gives background reasons for including neck strength and cervical function as injury-risk indicators when judging fighter pilots' fitness for high-G aircraft.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Measuring Neuromuscular Fatigue in Cervical Spinal Musculature of Military Helicopter Aircrew
authors: Michael F. Harrison; J. Patrick Neary; Wayne J. Albert; Usha Kuruganti; James C. Croll; V. Carol Chancey; Bradley A. Bumgardner
what_it_does: 40 military helicopter aircrew did maximal (MVC) and 70% MVC isometric neck endurance tests in extension, flexion and lateral flexion while EMG of splenius capitis, sternocleidomastoid and upper trapezius was recorded. The smaller agonist muscles fatigued most (splenius capitis about 21-22% in extension, sternocleidomastoid about 11-14% in flexion), while the trapezius showed no EMG fatigue.
why_useful: Informs the neck strength-endurance test protocol for helicopter aircrew, including which muscles limit force maintenance in each direction. The abstract gives no strength or endurance values, so it is a protocol reference, not a source of indicator values or norms.

title: Trampoline exercise vs. strength training to reduce neck strain in fighter pilots.

Both programmes reduced strain (sternocleidomastoid down 50% and 41%) with no significant difference between groups, and loading-test EMG stayed below baseline after 3 months of intensive high +Gz flying.

It concludes that the roles of strength training, muscle fatigue and aerobic fitness are less clear than some studies suggest, and that the effects of conditioning on G tolerance are not well established.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: Intra-rater reliability of electromyographic recordings and subjective evaluation of neck muscle fatigue among helicopter pilots
authors: Marcus Thuresson; Björn Äng; Jan Linder; Karin Harms-Ringdahl

what_it_does: 10 male helicopter pilots held 45-s isometric neck flexion and extension contractions at 75% of maximum strength, twice on the first day and twice more at one-week intervals, while surface EMG and Borg CR-10 fatigue ratings were recorded. The EMG median-frequency slope was acceptably reliable (ICC 0.65-0.83 at 45 s intra-day; 0.52-0.71 at 30 s) and subjective ratings were most reliable at 30 s inter-day (ICC 0.86-0.88), so the authors recommend a 30-s protocol.

section: Pilot and aircrew strength, fitness and flight demands
title: [Effects of extended flight factors on +Gz tolerance].
authors: Khomenko Mn; I. V. Bukhtiarov; Malashchuk Ls

full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request

what_it_does: After a 5-hour single-seat fighter flight simulation, 6 centrifuge test subjects (the abstract does not say whether they were pilots) were exposed to gradual-onset +Gz with muscle relaxation and no anti-G suit, and to complex 2.0-9.0 G profiles with suit and straining maneuvers. Results were compared with their own earlier tolerance data, with hemodynamics, leg muscular effort strength, and post-run respiration and gas exchange measured. The prolonged simulation impaired functional state and high +Gz tolerance: visual disturbances and cardiac arrhythmias became more frequent and severe, and energy expenditure and cervical muscle fatigue increased.

authors: David C. Myers; Deborah L. Gebhardt; Carolyn E. Crump; Edwin A. Fleishman
cautions: technical or government report, published before 2005
what_it_does: Predictive criterion-related validation of the Army's Military Entrance Physical Strength Capacity Test battery in 1,003 female and 980 male soldiers tested before basic training, against basic-training outcomes and lift, carry, push and torque criterion tasks completed by 951 soldiers after advanced individual training. Validity was high (R = .84): the Lift 60 explained 67% of criterion variance, with lean body mass and an upright pull adding 3% and 1%.
why_useful: A classic validation of a strength-based classification battery against job-task criteria, the evidence chain a strength-type classifier for pilots would need.

section: Physical aptitude classification, employment standards and pilot selection
title: Development of a multimodal magnetic resonance imaging-based machine learning prediction model for flight cadets
authors: Lu Ye; Shuhao Weng; LiYa Ba; Dongfeng Yan; Haiqing Si
what_it_does: Fused structural, diffusion-tensor and functional MRI features from 39 civil-aviation flight cadets with extensive flight training and 37 ground cadets, and trained logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine and Gaussian naive Bayes classifiers with five-fold cross-validation and permutation tests to tell the groups apart. The multimodal logistic regression model performed best (accuracy 0.838, AUC 0.942, sensitivity 0.835, specificity 0.834), and SHAP analysis linked the top features to higher cognitive function, visual processing and attention allocation.
why_useful: Offers a transferable template for the program's machine-learning and explainability layer (feature-level fusion, five-fold cross-validation, permutation testing, SHAP) in pilot candidates. Its predictors are brain MRI, not physical indicators, and it separates already-trained flight cadets from ground cadets rather than predicting selection or training outcomes.

section: Physical aptitude classification, employment standards and pilot selection
title: What Drives Army Fitness Testing Success? Analysis of Body Composition, Performance, and Predictive Measures Among ROTC Cadets
authors: Yosef Shaul; Megan Sax van der Weyden; Joel Martin
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Cross-sectional and longitudinal study of 177 ROTC cadets (134 male, 43 female) on sex differences in body composition and ACFT performance, performance quintiles and change over time. Hand-release push-ups and plank together predicted total ACFT score (R2=0.625) while body composition had limited predictive value overall (R2<=0.138); FFM and FFMI were more strongly linked to strength-power events in men; and rescoring under the sex-neutral AFT combat standard substantially changed failure rates and body-composition exemption eligibility, especially for female cadets.
why_useful: Informs strength-indicator choice, standard setting and fairness checks for pass/fail thresholds, showing how a switch to a sex-neutral standard shifts failure rates in a military cadet cohort.

section: Physical aptitude classification, employment standards and pilot selection
title: Mapping psychological heterogeneity in military cadets: a multi-method framework combining network analysis, latent profiles, and risk nomograms
authors: Charis Ntakolia; Vasiliki Yotsidi
what_it_does: Ninety-two military cadets completed the DASS-21, CD-RISC-25 and personality measures three times over five months; the data were analysed with measurement-invariance testing, graphical-LASSO network analysis, latent profile analysis and logistic-regression nomograms intended as screening tools. Five cadet profiles were identified (entropy .973), but profiles based on change scores agreed only moderately with them (adjusted Rand index .245), and the best nomogram (academic performance) reached a cross-validated AUC of .682.
why_useful: A transferable template for the typing and decision-support components: latent profile classification of military trainees, a stability check on the typology, and cross-validated screening nomograms, though with psychological rather than physical indicators.

section: Physical aptitude classification, employment standards and pilot selection
title: Explainable machine learning for age-specific talent identification in Chinese youth football
authors: Yan Tong; Jingyi Bi; Shixin Li; Luohang Chen; Chun Liu; Hengxin Chen
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
what_it_does: Age-group-specific XGBoost, random forest and logistic regression models were trained on multidimensional assessments (anthropometric, physical, technical, psychological, match) of 398 U8-U12 Chinese youth football players to predict coaches' provincial elite selection, tuned with 5-fold cross-validation and interpreted with SHAP. The best models reached test-set ROC-AUC 0.900-0.957, dribbling speed and standing long jump mattered at every age while psychological traits added little, and the U12 male model showed only fair agreement (kappa 0.269) when applied retrospectively to national selection data.
why_useful: Informs the selection decision-support layer: a template for interpretable ML selection models (cross-validated classifiers plus SHAP), checked against an independent selection outcome, though its predictors are not strength-based.

section: Physical aptitude classification, employment standards and pilot selection
title: An impact analysis for adverse bias in the new Royal Navy physical employment standard
authors: Mark Metcalfe; Joseph A Hogan; Adrian Allsopp; Steven D Powell
venue: WORK: A Journal of Prevention, Assessment & Rehabilitation
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Evaluated the early adverse-bias impact of the Royal Navy PES implemented in September 2024 (a functional movement circuit based on the strength and muscular-endurance demands of emergency seafaring tasks), using annual test data from 2990 personnel (15.3% female), pass rates, the 80% rule and Z-tests. The overall pass rate was 98.9%, males passed at 99.4-100% and females at 87.4-98.1% (lower particularly under 25 years), and no significant adverse bias was found.
why_useful: A worked example of 80%-rule and Z-test monitoring for adverse impact of a strength-based military standard, transferable to auditing a pilot strength classifier for sex or age bias.

section: Physical aptitude classification, employment standards and pilot selection
title: High-stakes psychomotor ability assessment: a military selection case study of practice effects in airplane tracking tasks
authors: Christopher Draheim; Ciara Sibley; Nathan Herdener; Aaron Cochrane; S. R. Melick; Kaylin Strong; Joseph T. Coyne
what_it_does: 146 Naval Flight Students and 119 enlisted Sailors did the psychomotor airplane-tracking tasks of the Navy's Aviation Selection Test Battery six times over two days. Practice effects were large, rank order shifted, and scores had not levelled off by the sixth attempt. Correlations with later flight-training scores held steady across attempts, but simulations showed predictive validity can vary widely when candidates have had different amounts of practice.
why_useful: Informs validation and decision-rule design for selection tests in a pilot-selection pipeline: practice and retest effects, stability of rank order, and predictive validity against training outcomes.

authors: Ebru Yazgan
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Combines a risk assessment matrix with the Analytic Hierarchy Process to flag unacceptable personality traits among commercial airline and military pilots and rank their relative importance as causes of pilot error. Lack of self-discipline and rule-consciousness ranked highest for commercial pilots, while lack of self-discipline, absent rule-consciousness, overconfidence and neuroticism dominated for military pilots.
why_useful: Offers a risk-matrix-plus-AHP template for ranking attributes by risk, with separate weightings for military and commercial pilots, which could be adapted to weight indicators in a composite evaluation. It covers personality only and does not build or test a selection, assignment or training tool.

authors: Gilvan V. da Silva; Gregory F. Zehner; Jeffrey A. Hudson

what_it_does: Compared the multivariate boundary-cases approach with the univariate percentile approach for specifying anthropometric requirements in flight deck design; the abbreviation list refers to a Brazilian pilots anthropometric database. The multivariate approach captured more subjects than the percentile approach, and the authors conclude it sets better anthropometric limits when several body dimensions must be considered together.
why_useful: A multivariate boundary-case method for setting body-size limits across several correlated dimensions, which could be adapted to define multivariate physical types. It is a cockpit-design method based on anthropometry, not strength, and it does not classify pilots for assignment.

authors: Piete E H Brown; Joanne L Fallowfield
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Surveyed 515 UK Royal Navy personnel (443 men, 72 women), who rated the physical demand, criticality and frequency of 25 common sea-going tasks on 1-5 scales; a priori criteria were used to shortlist the critical, physically demanding tasks for a future employment standard based on muscle strength and endurance. Ten tasks met the criteria (fire fighting, damage control, casualty handling, basic movement/transit), casualty handling was rated the most demanding, and sex- and age-based differences in ratings were equivocal.
why_useful: Informs the role-demand (job analysis) step with a survey method for identifying the critical strength- and endurance-demanding tasks that suitability standards should target.

authors: T. Reilly; M. Spivock; A. Prayal-Brown; B. Stockbrugger; R. Blacklock

what_it_does: Secondary analysis of 668 Canadian Armed Forces participants from the FORCE physical employment standard research, relating bioelectrical impedance body-composition measures and demographics to FORCE and Common Military Task Fitness Evaluation performance by correlation and linear regression. Lean body mass correlated strongly with lifting, pulling and carrying tasks (e.g. r = 0.78 for stretcher carry), and the authors conclude that lean and dead mass can help predict success on such tasks, although no minimum lean body mass is required.
why_useful: Informs indicator choice for the typing model by showing that body-composition measures (lean and dead mass) predict strength-dominant military task performance, and flags adverse-impact issues for standards built on anthropometrics.

title: A Task Analysis Methodology for the Development of Minimum Physical Employment Standards
authors: Richard D.M. Stevenson; Andrew G. Siddall; Philip F.J. Turner; James L.J. Bilzon
what_it_does: Developed a systematic task analysis process for setting minimum acceptable job performance in arduous safety-related occupations, applied to UK firefighters: all-male subject-matter experts identified critical, physically arduous tasks and built role-specific task simulations, and video footage with blinded voting set the minimum acceptable performance. Eight tasks with role-specific variations, suitable task simulations, and the matching minimum acceptable performance were identified.
why_useful: Informs the step that sets each role's criteria, with a structured expert-panel method (critical tasks, task simulations, blinded video voting) for defining the minimum acceptable performance against which suitability is judged.

authors: Gary L. Bowen; Todd M. Jensen; James A. Martin
what_it_does: Proposed a 12-item Comprehensive Airman Fitness measure for the U.S. Air Force, built from the mental, physical, social and spiritual fitness components of the Support and Resiliency Inventory, and tested it with confirmatory factor analysis. The results supported treating the components as parts of one total-fitness construct, and the measure was invariant across subgroups.
why_useful: Offers a statistical template (confirmatory factor analysis plus testing that the measure works the same across subgroups) for checking the structure and cross-group fairness of the program's composite fitness score.

title: Standard Cognitive Psychological Tests Predict Military Pilot Training Outcomes
authors: Raymond E. King; Thomas R. Carretta; Paul Retzlaff; Erica Barto; Malcolm James Ree; Mark S. Teachout
venue: Aviation Psychology and Applied Human Factors
what_it_does: Tested two cognitive tests (Multidimensional Aptitude Battery and MicroCog) as predictors of initial military pilot training outcomes (completion, grades, check rides, class rank) in samples of 5,582 to 12,924 trainees. After correcting for range restriction and criterion dichotomization, full-scale IQ and general cognitive functioning correlated .29 and .26 with training completion, below the validities reported for US Air Force pilot aptitude tests that also measure aviation knowledge and psychomotor skills.
why_useful: Informs validation design for selection recommendations: criterion validation against pilot training outcomes with range-restriction correction, plus benchmark validities to compare a physical-type model against.

authors: Stephen H. Courtright; Brian W. McCormick; Bennett E. Postlethwaite; Cody J. Reeves; Michael K. Mount
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Meta-analysis of male-female differences on physical ability tests used for selection and placement, testing selection-system design, measurement specificity and training as moderators. section: Physical aptitude classification, employment standards and pilot selection
title: International Paralympic Committee position stand—background and scientific principles of classification in Paralympic sport
authors: S M Tweedy; Y C Vanlandewijck
full_text_version: the issuing organisation's own edition of the same text
what_it_does: This IPC position stand sets out the scientific background of Paralympic classification, distinguishes performance from selective classification, and warns that the weighting and aggregation of measures threaten the validity of current systems. It defines an evidence-based classification system as one whose purpose is stated unambiguously and for which empirical evidence shows that the methods for assigning classes achieve that purpose, and names the lack of a clear statement of purpose as a major barrier.
why_useful: A framework from classification theory that transfers by analogy to building and defending a physical type-classification system: state what the types are for, show with data that the assignment method serves that purpose, and treat the weighting and aggregation of measures as a threat to validity.

section: Physical aptitude classification, employment standards and pilot selection
title: Occupational Relevance and Body Mass Bias in Military Physical Fitness Tests
authors: Paul Montgomery Vanderburgh
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser
what_it_does: A review arguing that US Army, Navy and Air Force fitness tests penalise larger, not just fatter, service members (a gap explained by biological scaling laws), although larger personnel do better on work tasks such as load carriage and lifting, for which lean mass and its ratio to fat plus external load are stronger determinants than push-up, sit-up or 2-mile run results. Because promotion partly depends on these tests, lighter personnel gain an advantage; proposed fixes (balanced tests, scaled scores, correction factors) mostly still need large-scale validation, and the author calls for research in women.
why_useful: Argues that unscaled military fitness scores carry a body-mass bias at odds with job-task performance and feed into promotion decisions, a fairness check for any composite score used to select or assign pilots.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Neuromuscular changes during a four-week individualized in-season strength-training program based on the dynamic strength index in youth basketball players: A quasi-experimental study
authors: Casado-Martínez P; Romero-Moraleda B; González-García J
what_it_does: Quasi-experimental study in which 21 youth basketball players were split by baseline dynamic strength index (DSI, from CMJ and isometric squat peak force) into high (>0.57), neutral or low (<0.45) tertiles, which received maximal-strength, mixed or ballistic/plyometric emphasis for four in-season weeks. The high tertile gained isometric peak force and estimated 1RM while its DSI fell, and the neutral tertile gained estimated 1RM; CMJ outcomes did not change significantly in any tertile, no significant interaction effects were observed, and the authors present the results as observational.
why_useful: Informs the strength-typing and training-recommendation parts of the program. It is a worked example of cutting a muscular-strength ratio index into types and giving each type a training emphasis. The sample is small, though, and no significant interaction effects backed the type-specific changes.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Quadrant training: a simple typology-based approach to improve strength and endurance in youth soccer players
authors: Timo Steidle; Benedikt Meixner; Mascha Lenk; Marcelle Schaffarczyk; Billy Sperlich
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
what_it_does: Non-randomized controlled study of male U16-U17 soccer players from two academies (intervention n = 38, control n = 22; academy and intervention effects are confounded). Players were classified into endurance quadrants (below or above the team mean on 30-15 IFT velocity and V4) and strength quadrants (relative isometric mid-thigh pull strength and CMJ height) and given quadrant-specific endurance training plus one weekly strength session; the intervention group improved V4, CMJ and IMTP within-group, but no between-group effect (strongest for CMJ, p = 0.020; none for IMTP; vIFT tending to favour controls) survived multiple-comparison correction, and the authors call the findings preliminary.
why_useful: Informs the strength-typing and training-assignment parts of the program. It offers a simple two-indicator quadrant typology (relative IMTP strength by CMJ height) that maps physical types to training. The allocation was tested against a control group, but the design was non-randomized and confounded by academy.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Strength, Jump Height, Landing, and Mobility Metrics Predict High and Low Performers of a Fire and Move Assessment: A Machine Learning Approach
authors: Ayden Mccarthy; Joel Thomas Fuller; Jodie Anne Wills; Steve Cassidy; Mita Lovalekar; Bradley C. Nindl; Tim L. A. Doyle
what_it_does: Thirty-four participants completed physical-quality tests and a combat fire-and-move assessment; exploratory factor analysis reduced strength, power, jump, landing and mobility measures to four factors (81.46% of variance), which were compared between high performers (50 laps) and low performers and used to train logistic regression, multilayer perceptron and random forest classifiers. All factors were higher in high performers, Factor 1 (isometric strength, jumping, drop landing) showed a very large effect (d = 2.15) and was the most influential feature, and logistic regression reached 100% test accuracy versus 86% for the other models.
why_useful: Informs the strength-based typing method: a template for reducing a strength, power and mobility battery to latent factors and classifying participants into high and low performers on a military task, with feature importance to justify indicator weighting. The abstract does not say the participants were soldiers, and 100% test accuracy from a 34-person sample should be cited with caution.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: The Influence of Sport Representation and Attitudes Toward Strength Training on Neuromuscular Performance Profiles in University Athletes: Part I Female Athletes
authors: Zachary J. McClean; Ricardo da Silva Torres; Walter Herzog; Kati Pasanen; Victor Lun; Sophia Nimphius; Matthew J. Jordan
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: In 192 female university athletes from five sports, results from a comprehensive lower-body neuromuscular performance testing battery were clustered into performance profiles, and Fisher's exact tests compared attitudes toward strength training across clusters. Three clusters emerged (high-strength/high-power/high-stiffness, low-strength/low-power/low-stiffness, low-strength/low-power/high-stiffness) that did not differ in sport representation but did differ in attitudes toward strength training.
why_useful: Informs the strength-based typing method. It is a worked example of clustering a multi-metric neuromuscular battery into readable strength/power/stiffness profiles that the authors propose as benchmarks. The subjects are athletes, and the abstract reports no validation or replication of the clusters.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Comparisons between different methods of calculating dynamic strength index: Effect on training recommendations
authors: Nicholas Joel Ripley; Jack Fahey; Stuart Guppy; Paul Comfort
what_it_does: Thirty-seven team-sport athletes performed countermovement jumps and isometric mid-thigh pulls on force plates. Peak-force DSI was compared with impulse-based DSI (matched to CMJ propulsion duration or fixed at 250 ms), each used to assign athletes by thresholds (>0.80, 0.60-0.80, <0.60) to maximal-force, balanced or dynamic-force training; fixed impulse DSI was significantly higher than the other methods, and training recommendations agreed for only 44.7% (peak-force vs matched) and 55.3% (peak-force vs fixed) of athletes, against 84.2% between the two impulse-based methods.
why_useful: Directly relevant to turning strength types into training recommendations. It shows that the calculation method behind a strength-typing index changes many individuals' assigned category, so the decision-support module must fix its index definition and justify it.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: The Influence of Sport Representation and Attitudes Toward Strength Training on Neuromuscular Performance Profiles in University Athletes: Part II Male Athletes
authors: Zachary J. McClean; Ricardo da Silva Torres; Walter Herzog; Kati Pasanen; Victor Lun; Matthew J. Jordan
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Applied unsupervised machine learning to a body-weight-normalised neuromuscular (strength, power and jump) test battery from 272 healthy male university athletes in 5 sports, using Fisher's exact tests to compare their attitudes toward strength training across clusters. Five neuromuscular profiles emerged (e.g., a high-strength/high-power cluster with a braking-dominant jump strategy and a large ice hockey representation), and attitudes differed across profiles (p < 0.05).
why_useful: Directly adaptable to the strength-based typing module: it shows how to cluster a normalised strength/power test battery into interpretable profiles that can serve as benchmarks.

title: Unsupervised Machine Learning in Countermovement Jump and Isometric Mid-Thigh Pull Performance Produces Distinct Combat and Physical Fitness Clusters in Male and Female U.S. Marine Corps Recruits
authors: Patrick A Peterson; Mita Lovalekar; Debora E Cruz; Elizabeth Steele; Bridget McFadden; Harry Cintineo; Shawn M Arent; Bradley C Nindl
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser

what_it_does: In 565 U.S. Marine Corps recruits (386 men, 179 women), k-means clustering of force-plate countermovement-jump relative peak power, isometric mid-thigh pull relative peak force and dynamic strength index produced performance clusters, and recruits of both sexes in cluster 2 significantly outperformed cluster 1 on every combat and physical fitness test event. Lower-extremity injury incidence was also compared between clusters, but that result is cut off in the abstract.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Effectiveness of an Individualized Training Based on Dynamic Strength Index on Sprinting, Jumping and Change of Direction Performance in Basketball Players: A Randomized Controlled Trial
authors: Jernej Pleša; Filip Ujaković; Ažbe Ribič; Chris Bishop; Nejc Šarabon; Žiga Kozinc
venue: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine
what_it_does: In 43 elite basketball players, the intervention group (n=27) was split by dynamic strength index (ratio of CMJ to IMTP peak force) into ballistic (DSI <=0.90, n=11) and strength (DSI >0.90, n=16) training groups for a five-week in-season resistance program, compared with a control group on a standard program (n=16). The intervention group improved significantly in 20-m sprint and 505 change-of-direction times, mainly in the strength subgroup, while the control group stayed the same or declined.
why_useful: A concrete precedent for typing individuals by a muscular-strength ratio (a DSI threshold) and sending each type to a different training track. This maps onto the strength-typing and training-recommendation modules.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Latent profile analysis of spinal deep muscle strength and physical fitness in elite Taekwondo athletes
authors: Jae-Hoon Lee; Taehwan Kim; Minchul Lee; Min-Seong Ha
venue: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
what_it_does: Cross-sectional study of 104 adolescent elite Taekwondo athletes that used latent profile analysis of spinal deep-muscle strength, measured at several angles on a Centaur 3D device, and compared body composition and fitness (grip, back and leg strength, endurance, flexibility, balance) across profiles. Five profiles emerged, two with higher body weight and skeletal muscle mass (one of them also with the highest grip, back and leg strength); spinal muscle strength was not significantly related to balance and did not consistently track general fitness.
why_useful: Provides a transferable latent-profile method for typing individuals by trunk (spinal) muscle strength measured at multiple angles, then profiling their whole-body strength, body composition and fitness. This is relevant to the strength-based physical-type classification module. Its finding that spinal-strength profiles did not consistently track general fitness suggests trunk strength carries information that general fitness tests may miss.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Body shape and performance on the US Army Combat Fitness Test: Insights from a 3D body image scanner
authors: Maria Smith; Dusty Turner; Charlotte Spencer; Nicholas Gist; Sarah Ferreira; Kevin Quigley; Tyson Walsh; Nicholas Clark; William Boldt; Justin Espe; Diana M. Thomas
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: In 239 U.S. Military Academy cadets, k-means clustering of 3D-scanner body circumferences at 20 sites produced five body-shape groups, and the 'V'-shaped male and larger male clusters scored highest on all Army Combat Fitness Test events except the 2-mile run. The authors conclude body shape relates to ACFT performance in more detail than sex alone.
why_useful: A k-means physical-typing template built on anthropometry rather than strength and checked against occupational fitness test events, which informs the typing method and the choice of typing variables.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Unsupervised Clustering Techniques Identify Movement Strategies in the Countermovement Jump Associated With Musculoskeletal Injury Risk During US Marine Corps Officer Candidates School
authors: Matthew B. Bird; Qi Mi; Kristen J. Koltun; Mita Lovalekar; Brian J. Martin; AuraLea Fain; Angelique Bannister; Angelito Vera Cruz; Tim L. A. Doyle; Bradley C. Nindl
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Clustered countermovement-jump kinetic and kinematic variables from markerless motion capture and embedded force plates in 668 US Marine Corps officer candidates (547 male, 121 female) into three movement-strategy clusters and compared musculoskeletal injuries during the 10-week Officer Candidates School. Lower-extremity and torso injury proportions differed by cluster (30.5% high-risk, 22.5% moderate-risk, 13.8% low-risk), with higher braking rate of force development and net impulses in the low-risk cluster and female candidates concentrated in the high-risk cluster.
why_useful: A transferable typing method for the strength-based classification step: unsupervised clustering of force-plate force-production (plus kinematic) jump variables into types linked to an outcome, with screening thresholds.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: The Application of Fuzzy Clustering Analysis in the Comprehensive Evaluation of Military Physical Quality
authors: 慧静 孙
cautions: not in English, no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Applies fuzzy clustering to three military fitness test indicators (5-km run for endurance, 100-m run for speed, pull-ups for strength) to classify grass-roots company soldiers, using statistics to choose the best classification. Soldiers were divided into five physical-quality categories; the abstract does not give the sample size.
why_useful: Informs the typing method: a simple fuzzy-clustering template for sorting military personnel into physical-quality types from endurance, speed and pull-up strength indicators.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Prediction of cadet basic training physical performance outcomes
authors: Christopher Ploch; Diana M Thomas; Bryan Adams; Dusty Turner; Adam Hug; Jason Suby; John E. Palmer; Kevin Bigelman
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
cautions: conference paper, no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Applied linear regression and unsupervised k-means clustering to Cadet Fitness Assessment and Cadet Basic Training test data from 8,886 US Military Academy cadets (82% male, classes of 2012-2021) to predict basic-training physical performance. The relationship between BMI and 2-mile run was weak (R2=0.07), although age, BMI and gender were significant predictors; BMI related more strongly to pull-ups (R2=0.47), and four clusters emerged, including one of poor runners and one with poor swim, push-up and sit-up performance.
why_useful: Informs the typing method and prediction models: shows cluster-based profiling of military trainees from fitness test events and cautions against BMI as a performance predictor. The clusters are described by run, swim, push-up and sit-up results rather than strength measures, and this is a meeting abstract with no full text.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Fight load index and body composition are most associated with combat fitness in female Marines
authors: Katelyn Fleishman Allison; Karen A. Keenan; Mita Lovalekar; Qi Mi; Kim Beals; Lt. Col. Lawrence C. Coleman; Bradley C. Nindl
venue: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Hierarchical cluster analysis of two Combat Fitness Test events in 294 male and female Marines produced two performance clusters, which were then compared on anthropometry, body composition, fight load index, aerobic/anaerobic measures and isokinetic/isometric strength. The lower-performing cluster was mostly women (66 women, 16 men), and its women had greater body fat and fight load index than every other subgroup, while men in the better cluster had greater knee-flexion strength than women in either cluster and greater ankle eversion/inversion strength than women in the lower cluster.
why_useful: A tactical example of deriving performance types by clustering (on Combat Fitness Test event times, not on strength itself) and then describing the types with strength and body-composition indicators, including how sex is distributed across them.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Effectiveness of an Individualized Training Based on Force-Velocity Profiling during Jumping
authors: Pedro Jiménez-Reyes; Pierre Samozino; Matt Brughelli; Jean-Benoît Morin
what_it_does: Assigned 84 subjects for 9 weeks of resistance training to an 'optimized' group (split into force-deficit, velocity-deficit and well-balanced subgroups by their jump force-velocity imbalance, FVimb), a non-optimized group on a common program, or a control group. All optimized subgroups improved jump height (12.7%, 14.2% and 7.2% for velocity-deficit, force-deficit and well-balanced), with marked FVimb reductions in the deficit subgroups, whereas results in the non-optimized group were more variable and unclear.
why_useful: Models the type-to-training-track logic for training recommendations: a force-velocity profile sorts people into force-deficit, velocity-deficit or balanced types, and each type gets its own prescription. Caveat: the types come from a jump-derived force-velocity profile rather than a direct maximal-strength test, and the reported outcome is unloaded squat-jump height only.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Strength Testing in the Air Force: Current Processes and Suggestions for Improvements
authors: Carra S. Sims; Chaitra M. Hardison; Maria C. Lytell; Abby Robyn; Eunice C. Wong; Erin Gerbec
tags: aptitude-classification, strength-typing-method, strength-measurement, decision-support, validation-standards, fairness
what_it_does: RAND evaluation of the usefulness, validity and fairness of the US Air Force Strength Aptitude Test, a physical strength test used since 1987 to screen and classify enlisted personnel into career specialties, including a review of its validity evidence and how cut scores are set. It concluded that strength testing is needed but that the SAT and the current processes for setting minimum entry requirements for some specialties may not be ideal, identified gaps in the evidence, and carried out two of three proposed research efforts.
why_useful: A real-world case of classifying enlisted air force personnel (not pilots) into specialties by strength, with a critique of validity, fairness and cut-score setting that bears directly on the program's strength-based aptitude classification and decision-support modules.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: The Dimensions of Human Physical Performance: Factor Analysis of Strength, Stamina, Flexibility, and Body Composition Measures
authors: David C. Myers; Deborah L. Gebhardt; Carolyn E. Crump; Edwin A. Fleishman
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Confirmatory and principal-axis factor analyses of a broad physical test battery in 206 adults (102 men, 104 women) supported a six-factor model (static, dynamic, explosive and trunk strength, stamina and flexibility) with a common factor structure for men and women. Body fat related to stamina and dynamic strength but not to the other abilities.
why_useful: A validated set of strength dimensions that can serve as the axes of a strength-based physical typing scheme.
review_trail: first rating 4 (search agent); second review 3; Manual review of the abstract recovered from OpenAlex.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Classifying Endurance Runners by Kinematics Strengthens Relationships of Muscle-Tendon Unit Function with Running Economy and Performance
authors: Yuuri Eihara; Momoka Kinoshita; Koshi Jotoku; Sumiaki Maeo; Hiroaki Kanehisa; Tadao Isaka
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: In 120 endurance runners (60 female), isokinetic knee extension/flexion torque and jump measures were summarized by PCA, runners were clustered by k-means on foot-strike angle and knee range of motion, and stepwise regressions compared cluster-specific with whole-cohort models. Whole-cohort correlations of muscle-tendon function with energy cost and performance were only weak to fair, but cluster-specific models significantly strengthened them (adjusted R2 = 0.159-0.595).
why_useful: Supports the strength-typing component by showing that sub-typing individuals before relating muscle-strength measures to performance gives stronger, type-specific models.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Classification of vertical jump performance categories in futsal using machine learning algorithms
authors: Diana Ximena Martínez-Arce; Laura Andrea Quintero-Palma; Jessica Quiceno-Henao; Dario Cuasapud-Arroyave; Jhonatan Betancourt-Peña; Wilfredo Agredo-Rodríguez; Jesus Alfonso Lopez-Sotelo
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
what_it_does: Fifty-one male futsal athletes performed CMJ, SJ and DJ on dual force plates (148 valid observations); four performance categories were derived by PCA of six biomechanical variables, and four ML classifiers were trained on independent force-time metrics using athlete-level group splits with grouped 5-fold and nested cross-validation. Logistic regression reached F1 0.830 and AUC 0.977 on the test set (grouped CV F1 0.770, AUC 0.941); CMJ peak power was the most influential predictor, and removing drop-jump variables cut F1 to 0.604.
why_useful: A transferable template for the typing and ML classification components: derive performance types from force-plate jump measures by PCA, then train interpretable classifiers with athlete-level grouped validation so repeated trials from one person do not leak into the test set. The measures are jump power and force metrics in futsal players and the types are derived internally, so the paper shows the pipeline rather than validated strength types.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Effect of force-velocity profile-based individualized vs. non-individualized strength training on force-velocity profiles and athletic performance: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Gaojun Li; Yang Shen; Junlei Lin; Wei Li
venue: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
what_it_does: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 6 studies comparing force-velocity (FV) profile-based individualized with non-individualized strength training in adults (7-10 weeks, 2 sessions per week). Individualized training showed significant advantages for F0 (g = 0.99), V0 (g = 0.78), FV imbalance (g = 0.60) and vertical jump height (g = 0.82), but not for Pmax or sprint performance, and heterogeneity was high.
why_useful: Evidence for the training-recommendation part of decision support: whether prescribing training by a strength-based force-velocity profile improves outcomes, and where it does not.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: The Effects of Force‐Velocity Profile‐Based Load Prescription on Muscle Power and Functional Performance in Velocity‐Deficient Older Adults
authors: Jolien Deboutte; Christophe Delecluse; Martine Thomis; Evelien Van Roie
venue: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
what_it_does: Force-velocity profiles of 80 adults aged 65 or over were measured on a pneumatic leg press and expressed as z-scores against a young reference group (n = 60), with a z-score gap of 1 or more defining a force or velocity deficit; because force deficits were rare (n = 4), velocity-deficient participants (57 started) were randomized to 12 weeks of training at loads matched or deliberately not matched to their deficit. Matched training increased V0 more and non-matched training increased F0 more, but changes in power and functional performance did not differ between groups.
why_useful: Offers a concrete norm-referenced rule for strength-based typing (force or velocity deficit from z-scores against reference values) and a randomized test of whether type-matched training prescriptions improve outcomes.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Vertical Force–Velocity Profiling in Soccer: A Systematic Review of Evidence, Assumptions, and Limitations
authors: Khairi Salim; El Mouahid Khalid; Chmura Paweł; Rfaki Abderrazak
venue: Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology
what_it_does: PRISMA systematic review of 11 studies on vertical force-velocity profiling in soccer. It found heterogeneous, task-dependent associations of F-V variables (notably Pmax and V0) with jump and sprint outcomes, distinct profiles by age, maturity, playing position and sex, and only limited, inconsistent evidence for individualized or deficit-based training prescription; it concludes that F-V profiling is a context-dependent descriptive framework rather than a mechanistic performance model.
why_useful: Warns the strength-typing and training-recommendation components how far force-velocity profiles can support role-specific typing or deficit-based prescription.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Anthropometric and motor-fitness signatures of defensive efficiency in professional football defenders: a principal component and cluster analysis
authors: Jeneviv Nene John; Sam Chidi Ibeneme; Gerhard Fortwengel; Emeka Mong; Davidson Okwudili John; Ezinne Olive Nwosu; Blessing Chidimma Okpagu; Nnenna Christiana Chinagozi-Amanze; Paul Onyeudo
venue: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
what_it_does: Ecological profiling of 36 professional defenders from one Nigerian Premier Football League club over three seasons, relating pre-season anthropometric and motor-fitness tests (agility, vertical-jump power, reaction time, balance, coordination) to team-level defensive statistics with correlations, PCA and k-means clustering, without individual-level regression. PCA gave three components explaining 72.5% of variance, and k-means found three defender archetypes (heavier, slower stoppers; leaner, faster coverage defenders; balanced hybrids) that differed most in agility.
why_useful: Offers a transferable PCA-plus-k-means recipe for deriving role-specific anthropometric and fitness archetypes, adaptable to defining pilot physical types, though its link to performance is only at team level.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Between Session Reliability of Traditional and Temporal Bilateral and Unilateral Dynamic Strength Index Calculations and Association With Sprint and Change of Direction Performance
authors: Jason Tallis; Lee Bolt; Rhys O. Morris; Timothy J. Suchomel; Steven J. Eustace
what_it_does: Thirty-eight recreationally active men completed 20-m sprints, 5-0-5 change-of-direction tests, bilateral and unilateral countermovement jumps and isometric mid-thigh pulls on two occasions. Traditional and time-based dynamic strength index (DSI) variants were analysed with Bayesian ICCs and with multiple linear regression after K-means clustering on DSI root metrics; between-session reliability was poor to moderate (ICC 0.24-0.76, highest for traditional DSI), links with sprint and change-of-direction performance were limited (strongest for dominant-side DSI100, R2 = 0.33-0.36, and better in participants with higher CMJ peak propulsive force), and the authors advise caution in using DSI for exercise prescription.
why_useful: A warning for the strength-typing module: dynamic strength index variants, which are strength-ratio indices used to profile individuals, showed only poor-to-moderate test-retest reliability (best for the traditional peak-force DSI) and weak links to sprint and change-of-direction performance. Any strength-ratio type therefore needs a reliability check. The paper also shows K-means clustering of individuals on strength root metrics.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Force-velocity profile based training to improve vertical jump performance a systematic review and meta analysis
authors: Paul Solberg; Will G. Hopkins; Vidar Andersen; Kolbjørn Lindberg; Thomas Bjørnsen; Atle Saeterbakken; Gøran Paulsen
what_it_does: Systematic review and meta-analysis (10 studies identified, 4 meta-analysed) comparing training optimized to correct vertical force-velocity profile deficits with non-optimized training. Optimized training partially corrected force deficits and fully corrected velocity deficits, but jump-height gains were comparable to non-optimized training and power effects were small to trivial, leaving the superiority of profile-based training unclear.
why_useful: Evidence for the decision-support module on whether assigning training by strength (force-velocity) profile type beats generic training; the abstract finds no clear advantage.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Effectiveness of Individualized Training Programs Based on the Optimal Force-Velocity Relationship to Develop Athletes’ Jump Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
authors: Zhaoqian Li; Peng Zhi; Xing Zhang; Junbei Bai; Amador García Ramos; Danica Janicijevic
what_it_does: Systematic review with meta-analysis comparing athlete training individualized to the force-velocity (F-V) profile against non-individualized programs. Individualized training reduced F-V imbalance more (SMD = 0.59) but did not significantly improve jump height (SMD = 0.50, p = 0.059) or maximal power overall, with a jump-height benefit only in athletes starting with a velocity deficit (SMD = 0.77).
why_useful: Shows that the benefit of profile-type-specific training depends on deficit type, useful for calibrating type-specific training recommendations in the decision-support module.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Development of Dynamic Strength Index Based on Free-Weight Exercises for Collegiate Male Sprinters
authors: Kentaro Chino; Hayate Tokuoka; Yoshihiko Ito
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Thirteen collegiate male sprinters had countermovement-jump and isometric mid-thigh-pull peak force measured on a force plate, plus 1RM in six free-weight lifts, to find free-weight substitutes for the dynamic strength index (DSI). Deadlift 1RM correlated best with IMTP peak force (r = 0.52) and squat-jump 1RM best with CMJ peak force (r = 0.69); their ratio correlated r = 0.56 with force-plate DSI and was proposed as a field alternative.
why_useful: Suggests a field route (free-weight 1RM) to approximating a strength-typing index where force plates are unavailable, though agreement is only moderate and the sample is very small.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Impact of a six-week training program on physical fitness and performance of young tennis players: a cluster analysis approach
authors: João P. Oliveira; Daniel A. Marinho; Tatiana Sampaio; Bulent Kilit; Jorge E. Morais
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
what_it_does: Clustered young tennis players aged 10-14 by International Tennis Number and physical fitness metrics before and after a six-week specific training program, and tracked changes in cluster membership (sample size not stated). Performance improved across clusters (ITN about 15%, 5-m sprint 8.5%, T-drill time 10%), but the variables driving cluster formation shifted and players moved between clusters in both directions.
why_useful: Informs how often the typing module should re-classify individuals, since cluster-based fitness types shifted after a short training block.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Individualized Training Based on the Force-Velocity Profile: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis examining the Effects on Motor Performance
authors: Christofer Wolte; Thomas Gronwald; Marcelle Schaffarczyk; Jan Wilke
what_it_does: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 included randomized controlled trials in healthy adults, comparing training individualized by force-velocity profile with non-individualized training lasting at least four weeks, pooled with robust variance estimation. It found no significant differences for strength (SMD -0.04), sprint time (SMD 0.28) or jump height (SMD 1.8), and concluded that FV-based individualization is not currently supported for performance gains.
why_useful: A caution for the training-recommendation part of decision support: assigning training by strength (force-velocity) profile has not yet been shown to beat non-individualized programs.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Is the Force–Velocity Profile for Free Jumping a Sound Basis for Individualized Jump Training Prescriptions?
authors: Maarten F. Bobbert; Kolbjørn Lindberg; Gøran Paulsen
what_it_does: Used a musculoskeletal simulation model of loaded squat jumps (four body segments, six muscle-tendon actuators) to test whether realistic changes in muscle properties or initial posture could reproduce the force-velocity profile changes reported after individualised training. They could not; because the profile was very sensitive to jump-height gains at low or at high loads, the authors argue that pre-training imbalances may reflect lack of skill, in which case individualised optimised training would neither transfer to other tasks nor outperform other training.
why_useful: Acts as a validity caution for the typing module: force-velocity-profile 'deficits' may reflect test skill rather than muscle capacity, so profile-based training tracks need independent validation.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Body composition as a marker of performance and health in military personnel
authors: Lynn Cialdella-Kam; Taylor K. Bloedon; Michael S. Stone
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
what_it_does: Review of 17 studies (2003-2023, drawn from 225 PubMed records) in military personnel with directly measured percent body fat, examining how body composition relates to physical and military-specific performance, to health, and to weight-control behaviours. Evidence linking body composition to operational readiness was limited, weight cycling and disordered eating were reported, and the authors call for research in women, racial and ethnic groups, and the Air Force and Navy.
why_useful: Informs whether and how body-composition measures should be weighted in a composite military fitness evaluation, noting weak evidence for their link to operational performance and possible harmful behaviour around the standards.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Clustering of football players based on performance data and aggregated clustering validity indexes
authors: Serhat Emre Akhanli; Christian Hennig
venue: Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports
what_it_does: Clusters mixed-type performance data on football players from eight major European leagues (2014-15 season) using a tailor-made dissimilarity measure, and chooses both the clustering method and the number of clusters by a weighted average of calibrated validity indexes picked to suit the aim of the clustering. Two clusterings are derived, major groups of players for analysing team composition and many small clusters (about 10 players each) for finding players similar to a given player, and the criterion weights for the second are informed by a survey of football experts.
why_useful: A worked sport example of choosing the clustering method and the number of clusters from several validity indexes weighted by the clustering's purpose, which transfers to choosing pilot types tied to the decisions they serve. Note that the data are match-performance statistics, not strength measures.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Clustering U-14 Portuguese regional team football players by lower limb strength, power, dynamic balance, speed and change of direction: understanding the field position factor
authors: Tatiana Sampaio; Daniel Marinho; José Eduardo Teixeira; João Oliveira; Jorge Morais
what_it_does: Cluster analysis of 22 U-14 male regional-team soccer players using jump-based lower-limb strength/power measures (countermovement jump, squat jump, reactive strength ratio), dynamic balance, 30 m sprint and change-of-direction tests. Three clusters emerged, driven mainly by the two jumps and the 30 m sprint, and no cluster was made up only of players from one field position.
why_useful: Shows how to check whether strength/power-based physical clusters line up with operational roles, analogous to testing pilot physical types against aircraft or role assignment.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Statistical power for cluster analysis
authors: Edwin S. Dalmaijer; Camilla L. Nord; Duncan E. Astle
what_it_does: Simulated power and classification accuracy of common clustering pipelines (k-means, hierarchical clustering and HDBSCAN, after no dimensionality reduction, MDS or UMAP), and directly compared k-means with fuzzy c-means and finite mixture models, varying subgroup size, number, separation and covariance. Power was sufficient with about 20 per subgroup only when separation was large (Δ = 4) and did not improve with more participants beyond a sufficient size, fuzzy clustering was more powerful at somewhat lower separation (Δ = 3), and the authors recommend 20-30 per expected subgroup and fuzzy or mixture-model approaches.
why_useful: Gives up-front guidance on sample size and choice of algorithm for typing pilots or cadets by clustering. The caution is that clustering has adequate power only when the types are expected to be clearly separated.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Should we individualize training based on force‐velocity profiling to improve physical performance in athletes?
authors: Kolbjørn Lindberg; Paul Solberg; Bent R. Rønnestad; Martin Thorsen Frank; Tommy Larsen; Gøran Abusdal; Sveinung Berntsen; Gøran Paulsen; Ole Sveen; Olivier Seynnes; Thomas Bjørnsen
venue: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser
what_it_does: Forty national-level team-sport athletes were randomised, based on their squat-jump force-velocity profile, to 10 weeks of training toward, away from, or irrespective of their theoretical optimal profile. No group differed significantly on sprint, jump, 1RM squat or leg-press power, and change toward the optimal profile correlated negatively with squat-jump gains (r = -0.49), so training individualised by profile was not supported.
why_useful: A randomised test of whether assigning training by a strength-power (force-velocity) profile does better than training that is not individualised. Its null result is a caution that type-based training recommendations should be tested against outcomes before a program adopts them.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Force-velocity profiling in athletes: Reliability and agreement across methods
authors: Kolbjørn Lindberg; Paul Solberg; Thomas Bjørnsen; Christian Helland; Bent Rønnestad; Martin Thorsen Frank; Thomas Haugen; Sindre Østerås; Morten Kristoffersen; Magnus Midttun; Fredrik Sæland; Gøran Paulsen
what_it_does: A multicentre study (27 male athletes in the main analysis, up to 82 male and female athletes on some measures) tested lower-limb force-velocity profiles from squat jump, countermovement jump and leg press twice before and twice after a 2-6 month period, comparing force plate, linear encoder and flight-time methods. Despite strong linearity (R2 > 0.95), the FV slope was unreliable in vertical jumping (CV 14-30%, ICC 0.36-0.79), only the leg press showed acceptable reliability, and agreement across methods was weaker for V0 and slope than for F0 and Pmax.
why_useful: Shows how to check whether a strength-derived typing variable, such as force-velocity slope, is reliable enough to assign types. It also shows that a profile with a good fit can still fail that check, and that the protocol matters (leg press versus jumps).

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: A method for developing organisation-wide manual handling based physical employment standards in a military context
authors: Greg L. Carstairs; Daniel J. Ham; Robert J. Savage; Stuart A. Best; Ben Beck; Daniel C. Billing
venue: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser
what_it_does: Presents a structured method for organisation-level, manual-handling-based PES in the multi-trade Australian Army: job task analysis of 57 employment specialisations identified 458 tasks, which were grouped into 10 movement-based clusters. The clusters informed a limited suite of tests that the authors describe as having high content, criterion and face validity and as implementable across a large organisation.
why_useful: A method for clustering tasks from many roles into a few movement-demand groups and a small test suite, adaptable to grouping aircraft types or pilot roles by strength demand; it clusters tasks, not personnel.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Interpreting Power-Force-Velocity Profiles for Individualized and Specific Training
authors: Jean-Benoît Morin; Pierre Samozino
venue: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Practical narrative guide for practitioners on obtaining and interpreting power-force-velocity profiles from simple field data (body mass, jump height, sprint times or velocity). It explains vertical profiling for jumps, including the optimal profile and force-velocity imbalance, and horizontal profiling for sprinting, illustrated with examples from the authors' practice.
why_useful: Supplies a measurement and interpretation framework for force-velocity profiling that could underpin strength-type definitions and individualised training recommendations.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Statistical Power to Detect the Correct Number of Classes in Latent Profile Analysis
authors: Jenn-Yun Tein; Stefany Coxe; Heining Cham
venue: Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser
what_it_does: A simulation of how well latent profile analysis recovers the true number of classes, varying class separation, true number of classes, sample size and number of indicators, and evaluating seven model-selection methods. No method had adequate power at small or medium separation (d = 0.2, 0.5); at very large separation (d = 1.5) the LMR, adjusted LMR, bootstrap LRT, BIC and sample-size-adjusted BIC selected well, at large separation (d = 0.8) power depended on the number of indicators and sample size, and AIC and entropy chose poorly in every condition.
why_useful: Guides sample size and number of indicators for latent profile analysis of continuous strength data. It points to the LMR test, bootstrap likelihood ratio test and BIC-type criteria, and warns against choosing the number of profiles by AIC or entropy.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Deciding on the Number of Classes in Latent Class Analysis and Growth Mixture Modeling: A Monte Carlo Simulation Study
authors: Karen L. Nylund; Tihomir Asparouhov; Bengt O. Muthén
venue: Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal
what_it_does: A Monte Carlo simulation compared likelihood-based tests and information criteria for choosing the number of classes in latent class, factor mixture and growth mixture models at n = 200, 500 and 1,000. BIC did best among the information criteria, and the bootstrap likelihood ratio test was the most consistent indicator across models.
why_useful: Simulation evidence for which indices to use (BIC among the information criteria, the bootstrap likelihood ratio test overall) when deciding how many types to keep, if strength-based types are derived by mixture modelling. It simulated only n = 200-1,000, so applying it to smaller pilot samples is an extrapolation.

section: Methods for deriving physical types from strength data
title: Stability-Based Validation of Clustering Solutions
authors: Tilman Lange; Volker Roth; Mikio L. Braun; Joachim M. Buhmann
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Introduces a cluster-stability measure of how well a clustering solution reproduces on a second sample, interpreted as a classification risk, and chooses the number of clusters by minimising that risk. The method gave convincing results on simulated and gene-expression data and performed competitively against other methods.
why_useful: If pilot physical types are derived by clustering strength indicators, this gives a check that the types reproduce in new data and a criterion for how many types to keep.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Decision-making model for cadet selection using the AHP TOPSIS method
authors: Tazky Tsany; Jonson Manurung; Muhammad Azhar Prabukusumo
what_it_does: Builds a cadet selection model for defense institutions: AHP weights seven criteria (academic potential test, academic interview, psychological test, ideological mental test, ideological mental interview, health test and physical test) and TOPSIS ranks candidates by closeness to an ideal cadet profile. The authors report the combined model is more objective, transparent and accountable than conventional assessment, but the abstract gives no sample size or validation.
why_useful: Informs the selection decision-support module with an AHP-TOPSIS weighting-and-ranking template that combines a physical test with health, psychological and academic criteria for military candidates.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: The Relationships Between Army Combat Fitness Test Performance and Functional Motor Competence in Army Reserve Officer Training Corps Cadets
authors: Madison S. Mach; Chris C. Cho; Hayley M. Ericksen; Brooke A. Slavens; Jennifer E. Earl-Boehm
full_text_version: the author's thesis on the same study, not the article itself
what_it_does: In 70 Army ROTC cadets (21 female, 49 male), standardized best attempts on long jump, ball throw and kick, and vertical jump were summed into a functional motor competence (FMC) composite and related to Army Combat Fitness Test scores by linear regression. FMC predicted ACFT total score (28.2% of variance) and each event score (6.7-22.6%), and the authors propose FMC screening to flag low-FMC cadets for extra neuromuscular training.
why_useful: Informs the composite-evaluation and early-screening components with a simple standardized field-test composite that predicts military fitness test performance and could route low scorers to extra training.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Optimization of a support vector regression model predicts maximal weight lifted during a manual material handling assessment within a military setting
authors: A. McCarthy; J.A. Wills; J.T. Fuller; E.D. Feigel; L. Rosenblum; B. Rawls; B.J. Martin; S. Cassidy; B.C. Nindl; T.L.A. Doyle
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Fifty-one general and military participants were assessed for physical characteristics and lift-to-place manual materiel handling performance, and previously developed support vector regression (SVR) and ridge models were retrained with hyperparameter and feature-selection tuning to predict maximal weight lifted. The best SVR models had lower prediction error than the best ridge models (RMSE 3.04 and 3.62 kg vs 3.32 and 4.24 kg).
why_useful: Informs the ML prediction and task-suitability components. It is a military example of predicting maximal lifting capacity from physical characteristics, which the authors suggest could ease personnel task selection. The sample mixes general and military participants.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Student-Pilot Error Prediction via Multimodal Physiological Signals and Tree-Based Models
authors: Gregory Barry; Chancellor Johnstone; William N. Caballero; Phillip R. Jenkins; Chun-An Chou; Yinan Wang; Christine Beauchene; Hrishikesh Rao; Nathan Gaw
venue: IEEE Transactions on Cognitive and Developmental Systems
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Built a machine-learning pipeline (mFLYER) that applies functional data analysis, feature selection and tree-based models to physiological and aircraft data recorded during student pilots' simulator landings. The study is framed around US Air Force pilot training and aims to predict flight errors and highlight the most predictive physiological modalities. The models improved on prior approaches and narrowed the gap between manual and automated grades, and calibrated models and ensembles were used to examine how confidently low- and high-error landings could be separated (sample size not stated).
why_useful: Informs the decision-support layer with an example of automated, uncertainty-calibrated ML assessment of military pilot trainees, although its predictors are physiological and flight data rather than strength or fitness measures.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Predicting Maximal Military Occupational Task Performance from Physical Fitness Tests Using Machine Learning
authors: Ayden Mccarthy; Jodie Anne Wills; Joel Thomas Fuller; Steve Cassidy; Brad C. Nindl; Tim L. A. Doyle
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Thirty-five participants completed two sessions of physical-characteristic testing (the abstract cites muscular strength, power, aerobic endurance and circumferences as such characteristics) plus military lift-to-place and jerry-can-carry assessments, and machine-learning models built on down-selected tests predicted the task outcomes. Support vector regression and ridge models predicted lift-to-place to RMSE ±1.77 kg and ±2.33 kg (NRMSE 4.44% and 5.84%) using four and three tests, while multilayer perceptron and SVR predictions of jerry-can-carry were weaker (±3.36 and ±3.67 laps; NRMSE 23.06% and 25.20%).
why_useful: Informs prediction-model design and indicator down-selection: a small set of physical tests predicted a role-specific military task outcome, with RMSE/NRMSE reporting the program could reuse. The abstract does not say whether participants were service members or how the models were validated.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: The Holistic Health and Fitness Management System (H2FMS): a modernised software capability for optimising soldier readiness and performance
authors: Andrew G Thompson; N A Rinaldi; C L Smith; K A Bigelman
what_it_does: Describes the requirements and design of the US Army's Holistic Health and Fitness Management System, a secure cloud-based platform that unifies biometric, performance-assessment, self-reported psychometric and existing-system data across physical, mental, spiritual, nutritional and sleep readiness domains. It uses automated support actions, role-based dashboards and integrated analytics to support H2F Performance Teams, soldiers and command teams; the abstract reports no evaluation data.
why_useful: Informs decision-support design: a real military example of routing fitness and health assessment results through role-based dashboards and automated actions to individuals, practitioners and commanders. It is a descriptive capability review with no decision rules or outcome data in the abstract, so cite it for system architecture, not as evidence that the platform improves readiness or injury outcomes.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Predicting special forces dropout via explainable machine learning
authors: Rik Huijzer; Peter de Jonge; Frank J. Blaauw; Maurits Baatenburg de Jong; Age de Wit; Ruud J. R. Den Hartigh
what_it_does: Compared four machine-learning models for predicting dropout among 274 special forces recruits (196 dropouts) from physical and psychological test scores, weighing predictive performance, explainability and stability. A stable rule-based SIRUS model was preferred (averaged AUC 0.70), and a higher 2800 m time, higher need for connectedness and larger skinfolds were most strongly associated with dropout.
why_useful: A template the program can adapt for an explainable, rule-based selection model built on physical and psychological test data, which informs the prediction-model and decision-support design.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: A machine learning framework to classify musculoskeletal injury risk groups in military service members
authors: Matthew B. Bird; Megan H. Roach; Roberts G. Nelson; Matthew S. Helton; Timothy C. Mauntel
what_it_does: In 4,222 U.S. Army Service members, survival machine-learning models (Cox regression, Cox with splines, conditional inference trees, random forest) were trained on self-reported injury-risk screens and health-record data (75% train, 25% test) to predict musculoskeletal injury over 30 to 365 days, with Cox regression best (time-dependent AUC 0.73 to 0.70 at 30 and 180 days). Binning predicted risk into quartiles gave a highest-risk group with an injury incidence rate ratio of 4.74 versus the lowest at 180 days.
why_useful: Shows how to build a risk model for military personnel, test it on held-out data and turn predicted probabilities into screening tiers, which informs prediction-model and decision-support output design.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: The Value of Strength as a Predictor of Musculoskeletal Injury in Canadian Armed Forces Basic Infantry Candidates
authors: Eric Robitaille; Tara Reilly; Scott Heipel; Hollie Buttici; Etienne Chasse; Hans Christian Tingelstad
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: In 129 Canadian Armed Forces basic infantry candidates, baseline questionnaires, anthropometry and physical tests (ankle dorsiflexion, Y-Balance, isometric mid-thigh pull, FORCE evaluation) were related to diagnosed musculoskeletal injuries with a backward stepwise logistic regression built on a development sample (n = 98) and applied to a validation sample (n = 33). Uninjured candidates scored significantly better on relative mid-thigh pull, FORCE 20 mR, FORCE ILS and estimated VO2peak; the final model results are cut off in the abstract.
why_useful: Supports using relative isometric mid-thigh pull strength and FORCE occupational fitness test scores as injury-risk indicators in military trainees. It also shows a development/validation split for a risk prediction model, though the truncated abstract does not give the final model's performance.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Low psychological resilience and physical fitness predict attrition from US Marine Corps Officer Candidate School training
authors: Jennifer N. Forse; Kristen J. Koltun; Matthew B. Bird; Mita Lovalekar; Evan D. Feigel; Elizabeth J. Steele; Brian J. Martin; Bradley C. Nindl
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Of 1006 US Marine Corps Officer Candidates School candidates (79.5% male) who gave blood, demographic, psychological and two fitness-test data, 260 (25.8%) attrited during the 10-week course, most often for musculoskeletal injury (30%). Sex, BMI, resilience, initial physical fitness test score, combat fitness test score and prior service were each associated with attrition, and the final backward-stepwise logistic model, assessed by ROC AUC, retained combat fitness test score and resilience.
why_useful: Shows fitness test scores combined with a psychological measure in a screening model for training attrition in a large military cohort. Informs prediction-model design and early-screening decision support, but the abstract gives no AUC value or validation.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Comparison of optimized machine learning approach to the understanding of medial tibial stress syndrome in male military personnel
authors: Vahid Sobhani; Alireza Asgari; Masoud Arabfard; Zeynab Ebrahimpour; Abolfazl Shakibaee
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Cross-sectional study of 180 male military recruits (30 with medial tibial stress syndrome, 150 without) that applied Bayesian-optimised ML classifiers to 25 demographic, anatomic and anthropometric predictors under under-, over- and no-resampling experiments. Ensemble and SVM models reached up to 100% performance with resampling, while without resampling Naive Bayes on 12 features gave accuracy 88.89%, sensitivity 66.67%, specificity 95.24% and AUC 0.8571.
why_useful: Example of ML injury classification from anthropometric and anatomic indicators in a military population, useful for the injury-risk component and as a caution about class imbalance and resampling in model validation.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Identifying special operative trainees at-risk for musculoskeletal injury using full body kinematics
authors: Lance Frazer; Tylan Templin; Travis David Eliason; Cody Butler; Ben Hando; Daniel Nicolella
what_it_does: Screened 156 male US Air Force special operative trainees with a markerless motion-capture system during functional movements, reduced the kinematic time-series with PCA and UMAP, and used semi-supervised and supervised approaches to identify trainees at risk of musculoskeletal injury. Trainees in the high-risk cluster had nearly five times the injury risk of those in the low-risk cluster, and the supervised model reached AUC 0.74 in leave-one-out analysis.
why_useful: Shows cluster-based risk typing plus a cross-validated supervised model built on automated movement screening in a military population, informing the typing method, automated assessment and injury-risk prediction.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Biomechanical and Psychological Predictors of Failure in the Air Force Physical Fitness Test
authors: Jeffrey Turner; Torrey Wagner; Brent Langhals
what_it_does: Applied logistic regression and a limited-capacity neural network to a 21-feature dataset (mental and social health survey, body composition, physical performance) from 223 active-duty US Air Force Airmen to predict fitness test failure. On a holdout set, logistic regression reached 0.84 accuracy (AUC 0.89) and the neural network 0.93 accuracy (AUC 0.97); poor sleep, recent injury, higher BMI and low fitness satisfaction marked higher failure risk.
why_useful: A template for the prediction-model component: an interpretable logistic baseline plus a neural network on mixed physical and psychological features, evaluated on holdout data in an Air Force population.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
