title: Optimized machine learning approach may improve understanding of medial tibial stress syndrome in military male personnel
authors: Vahid Sobhani; Alireza Asgari; Abolfazl Shakibaei
cautions: preprint, not peer reviewed, no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Cross-sectional study of 180 male military recruits (30 with medial tibial stress syndrome, 150 without) that used Bayesian optimization to select and tune ML classifiers on 25 demographic, anatomic and anthropometric predictors, with three experiments to handle class imbalance. Ensemble and SVM models reached up to 100% performance in experiments 1 and 3 (using at least 6 and 10 top predictors respectively), and Naive Bayes with the 10 most important features reached 88.89% accuracy, 66.67% sensitivity and 95.24% specificity in experiment 2.
why_useful: Preprint of r502 (BMC Research Notes 2023), which should be cited instead. Its use is the same: an example of ML injury-risk classification from anthropometric indicators in military personnel, mainly instructive on class imbalance. The perfect-performance claims rest on only 30 cases and call for caution.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Development and Validation of a Dynamically Updated Prediction Model for Attrition From Marine Recruit Training
authors: Iris Dijksma; Michel H.P. Hof; Cees Lucas; Martijn M. Stuiver
what_it_does: Built a landmark Cox proportional-hazards 'supermodel' from longitudinal data on 744 Dutch Marine recruits, using 21 predictors covering baseline characteristics and time-varying mental and physical health status to give personalised, weekly updated dropout probabilities. Under 10-fold cross-validation the c-index was 0.78, 0.75 and 0.73 at weeks 1, 4 and 12.
why_useful: Informs prediction-model and decision-support design: a template for dynamically updated individual risk estimates during military training, with cross-validated discrimination reported. The abstract names no fitness test scores among the predictors, and the authors say the model needs further validation in other military settings.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Using Machine Learning to Predict Lower-Extremity Injury in US Special Forces
authors: Christopher Connaboy; Shawn R. Eagle; Caleb D. Johnson; Shawn D. Flanagan; Qi Mi; Bradley Charles Nindl
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Prospective cohort of 140 US Air Force Special Forces operators tested at baseline for body composition, isokinetic strength, flexibility, aerobic/anaerobic capacity, anaerobic power and single-leg landing biomechanics, with lower-extremity injury tracked for 365 days and analysed with a CHAID decision tree. 27% were injured; a >25.1% difference in maximum knee flexion angle was most strongly associated with injury (69.2% injury rate), and all 7 such operators weighing >81.8 kg were injured.
why_useful: Informs injury-risk prediction and decision-support design: an interpretable decision-tree method that sets population-specific cut-points from physical test data in an Air Force special operations population.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Evidence-based information fusion platform for estimation of forest fire pilot fitness for duty
authors: Marie Lynn Reid
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser
what_it_does: Thesis that built an evidence-based information-fusion platform estimating a fit-for-duty index for forest-fire pilots from subjective, cognitive, physiological and sleep measurements, collected daily from 14 Conair pilots over the 2018 wildfire season, to help decision makers and planners assess their pilots.
why_useful: A worked example of fusing several daily measures into one fit-for-duty index for pilots to support duty decisions, the decision-support pattern the program needs, built on fatigue rather than strength.
review_trail: first rating 4 (search agent); second review 3; Manual review of the abstract recovered from OpenAlex.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: U.S. Army Physical Demands Study: Development of the Occupational Physical Assessment Test for Combat Arms soldiers
authors: Stephen A. Foulis; Marilyn A. Sharp; Jan E. Redmond; Peter N. Frykman; Bradley J. Warr; Deborah L. Gebhardt; Todd A. Baker; Maria C. Canino; Edward J. Zambraski
venue: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser
what_it_does: Used concurrent-validation data from 838 U.S. Army soldiers (608 men, 230 women) who completed Combat Arms criterion task simulations and up to 14 predictor tests, applying stepwise regression to build physical test batteries that predict task-simulation performance. Three batteries were developed (Test Battery 1: medicine ball put, squat lift, beep test, standing long jump and arm ergometer, adjusted R² 0.80-0.85); Test Battery 2 was adopted as the Occupational Physical Assessment Test because it was highly predictive, needed no complex equipment and covered a range of fitness domains.
why_useful: Informs indicator selection and the scoring model by showing how regression was used to choose a test battery that includes strength tests and predicts job-task performance for pre-employment screening.
notes: The USARIEM technical report on the same study (Development of the Occupational Physical Assessment Test (OPAT) for Combat Arms Soldiers, 2015) is in this list with its PDF.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: A Simplified Model to Predict Stress Fracture in Young Elite Combat Recruits
authors: Daniel S. Moran; Aharon S. Finestone; Yael Arbel; Nogah Shabshin; Arie Laor
venue: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Built a simple prediction model for stress fracture in 57 young male elite combat recruits measured before basic training (anthropometry, blood, fitness tests, pQCT bone quality, psychological, nutritional and activity history); aerobic training frequency, aerobic training duration and waist circumference correctly classified 85% of recruits. In a separate cohort of 59 recruits the model correctly classified 76.5%.
why_useful: Informs injury-risk prediction and validation: a simple risk equation from pre-training measures in a military population, tested on a second cohort.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Effect of Time Since Baseline Data Collection, Mechanism of Injury, and Service Academy Sub-population on Concussion Risk Prediction in Military Service Academy Cadets and Midshipmen: An Observational Study
authors: Yili Wang; Kenneth L. Cameron; Michael A. McCrea; Thomas McAllister; Steven Broglio; Mariel Lavieri; James T. Eckner; The CARE Consortium Investigators; Patrick O’Donnell; Kevin Bernstein; Adam Susmarski
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Applied eXtreme Gradient Boosting to CARE Consortium baseline assessments from 16,642 cadets and midshipmen at four U.S. military academies (2015-16 to 2019-20) to predict concussion in the following academic year, comparing sub-populations and injury mechanisms and ranking the most influential variables. Overall prediction performance fell from 0.68 to below 0.64 as time since baseline grew, and predictions were more accurate for intramural cadets and for military training or PE injuries than for varsity/club athletes and sport-related concussions.
why_useful: Transferable to injury-risk modelling and retest scheduling: in a large military cadet cohort, ML predictions from baseline testing lost accuracy as time since testing grew and differed by sub-population and injury mechanism. The abstract names no fitness or strength measures among the baseline concussion-testing predictors and describes no held-out validation, so the paper offers method lessons rather than fitness indicators.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Image-Based Evaluation System for Paraná State Military Physical Fitness Test: Pull-Ups
authors: Andrio Santos; Mauro Smaniotto; Fabio Schneider
venue: Proceedings of the 19th International Joint Conference on Biomedical Engineering Systems and Technologies
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser
cautions: abstract unavailable, summarised from the title, conference paper
what_it_does: Abstract unavailable; by title, presents an image-based system for evaluating the pull-up event of the Paraná State Military physical fitness test.
why_useful: May inform automated camera-based scoring of a strength-endurance test event in the program's assessment layer, once the full text is checked.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Limitations of linear load-velocity modeling for bench press performance in youth elite athletes
authors: Sebastian Puschkasch-Möck; Martin Hillebrecht; Michael Keiner; Carl-Maximilian Wagner; Andreas Konrad; Konstantin Warneke
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Fifty-three youth elite athletes did bench press one-repetition maximum (1RM) testing and a standardized load-velocity protocol, and linear regression load-velocity models were compared with neural network models for bias, agreement with measured 1RM and estimation error. Linear models underestimated maximal strength, while neural networks reduced bias and error, which points to a nonlinear load-velocity relationship in this population.
why_useful: Informs the strength-measurement module: estimating maximal-strength indicators from load-velocity data may need nonlinear (neural network) models rather than linear profiles.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Artificial neural network predictive models for optimizing the training process in race walking: a longitudinal observational study
authors: Dariusz Skalski; Magdalena Prończuk; Kinga Łosińska; Petr Stastny; Adam Maszczyk; Adam Zajac
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Thirty nationally ranked female race walkers were tested over four seasons (2021-2024) on ergospirometry, blood lactate, heart rate, gait kinematics and lower-limb strength (1RM, maximal power), and multiple and polynomial regression were compared with multilayer perceptron (MLP) and radial basis function (RBF) neural networks for predicting competitive performance. The RBF network predicted best (R2 = 0.89, RMSE = 0.28; MLP R2 = 0.87; regression R2 = 0.61-0.81), and heart rate, step length, VO2max and 1RM were the most influential predictors.
why_useful: A transferable example for the ML prediction module of combining a strength indicator (1RM) with physiological and gait measures in neural-network models that predict performance and guide training.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Machine Learning Applications in Non-Contact Lower Limb Sports Injury Prediction: A Systematic Review
authors: Jin Yuan; Quanwen Zeng; Anjie Wang; Yong Zhang; Jun Li
venue: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine
what_it_does: A PRISMA 2020 systematic review with PROBAST risk-of-bias assessment included 15 of 92 studies that used machine learning to predict non-contact lower-limb injuries, mostly in adult basketball and football athletes. Random forest and logistic regression were the most common methods, tree-based methods performed best in 6 studies (highest AUC 0.91, from a CHAID decision tree), and 87% of studies addressed model interpretability.
why_useful: Informs the injury-risk prediction component on typical algorithms, achievable performance, interpretability practice and the need for prospective validation.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Comparative analysis of machine-learning methods for prediction of pilot performance during startle events from neuropsychophysiological features of stress resilience and cognitive task scores
authors: Mate Gambiraža; Siniša Popović; Matej Kurtak; Krešimir Ćosić
what_it_does: Fifteen military pilot cadets completed laboratory tests of neuropsychophysiological stress-resilience features and cognitive tasks, then a flight-simulator task with unexpected perturbations; pitch-tracking error was predicted with multiple regression and machine-learning regression models under leave-one-out cross-validation, with preprocessing and feature selection inside the training folds. Under a fixed domain-balanced feature strategy a regression neural network did best (mean absolute error about 2.07 degrees, correlation about 0.75) against the regression baseline (2.55 degrees, about 0.70), but the gain was modest, feature-selection strategy mattered more than model type, and startle-related and allostatic features contributed most.
why_useful: A careful template for small-sample machine learning on pilot cadets: feature selection inside folds, leave-one-out validation, an interpretable baseline and ablation by feature domain. It also found that interpretable models were nearly as accurate as complex ones. This informs how the program should validate and explain its models, though the predictors and outcome are not physical fitness.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: A TabNet-SHAP framework with stability-weighted multi-method feature selection for muscle injury prediction in professional football
authors: Wenbo Rao
what_it_does: Builds a strictly prospective muscle-injury prediction framework for professional footballers from 438,219 Transfermarkt player-season records (15 seasons, 32 leagues), using stability-weighted multi-method feature selection, cost-sensitive learning and a chronological hold-out test on the two latest seasons. TabNet gave the best AUC, 0.812 (XGBoost 0.806, logistic regression 0.761), and SHAP ranked injury history as the top feature category (33%), ahead of market-and-career features (29%).
why_useful: Informs prediction-model design and validation for injury or duty-limitation outcomes: stability-verified feature selection, class-imbalance handling, chronological hold-out testing and layered SHAP interpretation.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: The application of machine learning in the prediction of sports injuries: systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Sijie Lou; Houwei Zhu; Zhanyang He; Binyong Ye; Gang Sun; Cuimei Shen
what_it_does: Systematic review and bivariate meta-analysis of 10 machine-learning sports-injury prediction models from 10 studies (five databases searched to December 2025). Pooled sensitivity was 0.79 and specificity 0.71 (diagnostic odds ratio 9.02), with sample size, model type, validation method and injury type named as possible influences; the authors recommend imbalance handling, k-fold cross-validation and adding time-series data.
why_useful: Gives benchmark accuracy figures and validation-design recommendations (imbalance handling, k-fold cross-validation) for any injury-risk prediction module in the program.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Biomechanical and movement-quality predictors of lower-limb load-related injury in collegiate athletes: a prospective cohort study using functional movement screening, wearable inertial sensing, and explainable machine learning
authors: Xuqingfeng Xu; Jihe Zhang; Jianlu Liao
what_it_does: Prospective one-season cohort of 161 collegiate athletes that combined Functional Movement Screen task scores with wearable inertial-sensor features in four classifiers under nested five-fold cross-validation with embedded LASSO; 37 load-related time-loss injuries occurred (23.0%). The fused XGBoost model reached an out-of-fold AUC of 0.70, versus 0.62 for FMS-only and 0.64 for wearable-only models, and biomechanical features added 0.07 AUC beyond prior-injury history.
why_useful: Informs injury-risk model design and realistic performance expectations: fusing screening-test and wearable features, nested cross-validation with embedded feature selection, and testing incremental value over prior injury.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Association of allostatic load measured by allostatic load index on physical performance and psychological responses during arduous military training
authors: Evan D. Feigel; Kristen J. Koltun; Mita Lovalekar; Christopher K. Kargl; Matthew B. Bird; Jennifer N. Forse; Varun J. Patel; Brian J. Martin; Elizabeth F. Nagle; Karl E. Friedl; Bradley C. Nindl
what_it_does: In 31 military personnel (14 women) on a 10-week arduous training course, related the change in an allostatic load index (0-8, built from neuroendocrine, autonomic and immune biomarkers) to changes in Physical Fitness Test scores, sleep difficulty, perceived stress and resilience, using simple and backward stepwise regression. In men, rising ALI was associated with falling pull-up, push-pull and total PFT scores, explained by immune components; in women it was associated with improved sleep-difficulty and resilience scores.
why_useful: Shows how a composite physiological-load index can be linked to fitness-test change in military trainees, which bears on readiness or training-load monitoring within a comprehensive fitness evaluation.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Machine Learning-Driven Muscle Fatigue Estimation in Resistance Training with Assistive Robotics
authors: Jun-Young Baek; Jun-Hyeong Kwon; Hamza Khan; Min-Cheol Lee
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Thirty-two men (64 limb datasets) performed seven isokinetic bench-press sets at a 7RM load while load-cell force-time data and RPE were recorded, and machine-learning models were trained on extracted and engineered biomechanical features to predict RPE. Engineered features reflecting relative fatigue progression improved prediction, and a random forest placed more than 93% of predictions within ±1 RPE unit.
why_useful: Informs automated processing of strength-test signals: shows how engineered features from force-time curves can feed a random-forest model, a technique adaptable to extracting indicators from dynamometer data.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Prediction of dynamic strength index (DSI) using one low-cost 2D video camera: a machine learning approach
authors: Mostafa Haj Lotfalian; Ali Abbasi
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: In 263 healthy participants performing countermovement jumps and isometric mid-thigh pulls, supervised regression models used six spatiotemporal features from a single 2D video plus height and weight to predict the Dynamic Strength Index, with isometric force from a back-and-leg dynamometer and force-plate data as ground truth. Gaussian process regression and neural networks were most accurate (R² > 0.92, RMSE < 0.06).
why_useful: Informs automated measurement of a strength-profile indicator: a low-cost video-plus-ML route to the Dynamic Strength Index (ballistic vs isometric peak force) that could serve as an input to strength-based typing.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Prediction of ACL injury incidence and analysis of key features in basketball players based on multi-algorithm models
authors: Longfei Guo; Zhilei Cui; Wei Ping Loh; Shazlin Shaharudin
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: In 104 male collegiate basketball players followed for 12 months (11 ACL injuries), variables that differed between injured and uninjured players (profile, physical function, sport skills, biomechanics, EMG during unanticipated side-cutting) were used to train several machine-learning models. AUC-ROC ranged from 0.66 to 0.80, with random forest best (0.80), and the most influential features were emergency-stop knee flexion moment and angle, backward ground reaction force and vastus lateralis activation.
why_useful: Informs injury-risk prediction modelling: a prospective ML template with AUC reporting, whose univariate feature pre-selection and few injury cases are design cautions for the program's own models.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Machine learning for classifying chronic ankle instability based on ankle strength, range of motion, postural control and anatomical deformities in delivery service workers with a history of lateral ankle sprains
authors: Ui-jae Hwang; Oh-yun Kwon; Jun-hee Kim; Gyeong-tae Gwak
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Cross-sectional study of 121 delivery service workers with a history of lateral ankle sprain (screened from 289) that trained and tested seven ML algorithms on PCA-derived components (7 PCs, 83.5% of variance) of ankle strength, range of motion, postural control and anatomical deformity measures to classify chronic ankle instability. SVM performed best (AUC = 0.817), and permutation importance and SHAP pointed to components related to BMI and ankle muscle strength.
why_useful: Offers a transferable explainable classification pipeline (PCA feature extraction, several classifiers compared by AUC, SHAP and permutation importance) on strength-inclusive physical measures, relevant to the typing method and to explaining model outputs.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: A Classification of Fitness Components in Elite Alpine Skiers: A Cluster Analysis
authors: Gabriella Penitente; Hayden A. Young; William A. Sands; Jeni R. McNeal
venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
what_it_does: Exploratory secondary analysis that uses hierarchical cluster analysis to group physiological and biomechanical fitness components (variables, not athletes) of elite alpine skiers, compared by sex and by world-cup versus non-world-cup level; the abstract gives no sample size. The components separated in the dendrograms of world-cup men and women but not of non-world-cup skiers; aerobic and anaerobic capacity components clustered tightly in most subgroups, and lower-body explosive force appeared more critical in male than in female world-cup skiers.
why_useful: Shows how cluster analysis of a multi-component fitness battery can reveal which components matter by sex and performance level, which helps choose indicators for the composite evaluation and the typing scheme.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: An Overview of Machine Learning Applications in Sports Injury Prediction
authors: Alfred Amendolara; Devin Pfister; Marina Settelmayer; Mujtaba Shah; Veronica Wu; Sean Donnelly; Brooke Johnston; Race Peterson; David Sant; John Kriak; Kyle Bills
what_it_does: Literature review of 42 original studies (2017-2022) that applied KNN, K-means, decision tree, random forest, gradient boosting, AdaBoost and neural-network models to sports injury prediction and prevention. Concludes that the lack of open, uniform datasets and reliance on dated regression models mean no strong conclusions about ML's real-world efficacy can yet be drawn.
why_useful: Background for the injury-risk prediction module, listing ML algorithms tried in sport and flagging the data and validation gaps the program should avoid.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Just How Confident Can We Be in Predicting Sports Injuries? A Systematic Review of the Methodological Conduct and Performance of Existing Musculoskeletal Injury Prediction Models in Sport
authors: Garrett S. Bullock; Joseph Mylott; Tom Hughes; Kristen F. Nicholson; Richard D. Riley; Gary S. Collins
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Systematic review (to June 2021) of 30 studies containing 204 musculoskeletal injury prediction models in sport built with regression, machine learning or both. No model was externally validated, 98% of models had high or unclear risk of bias, only 47% of studies did internal validation and 7% reported calibration, so no model could be recommended for practice.
why_useful: Sets out the validation and reporting requirements the program's injury and fitness prediction models should meet (a priori sample size, internal and external validation, discrimination and calibration, published equations or code).

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Force plate vertical jump scans are not a valid proxy for physical fitness in US special warfare trainees
authors: W. Casan Scott; Ben R. Hando; Cody R. Butler; John D. Mata; Jacob F. Bryant; Siddhartha S. Angadi
what_it_does: In 643 US Air Force Special Warfare trainees tested at entry and exit of an 8-week preparatory course, compared Sparta force-plate vertical-jump scan metrics with the eight-component Candidate Fitness Test (strength, power, muscular endurance, swimming, cardiovascular fitness) using paired t-tests and correlations. Jump-scan metrics declined slightly while most fitness-test measures improved, their changes were unrelated (r2 0.00-0.03), and the Sparta Score was not correlated with rucking or swimming and only weakly with the standing broad jump.
why_useful: A transferable caution for indicator selection and validation. In a large tactical sample, a single automated force-plate jump score did not track a multi-domain fitness battery, which argues against using it as a proxy for direct strength and fitness tests.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: The Use of Fitness Testing to Predict Occupational Performance in Tactical Personnel: A Critical Review
authors: Robin Orr; Takato Sakurai; Jordan Scott; Jason Movshovich; J. Jay Dawes; Robert Lockie; Ben Schram
venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
what_it_does: Critical review of 15 studies (rated 8.4/12 on the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme checklist) linking fitness-test results to job-task performance in tactical personnel. No standardized fitness test determined job performance; aerobic and anaerobic fitness, strength, endurance, power and agility were all associated with task performance, so a wide range of tests based on each unit's job demands appears necessary.
why_useful: Supports indicator selection and a multi-test battery built around the physical demands of each specific job.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Can Injuries Be Predicted by Functional Movement Screen in Adolescents? The Application of Machine Learning
authors: Josip Karuc; Marjeta Mišigoj-Duraković; Marko Šarlija; Goran Marković; Vedran Hadžić; Tatjana Trošt-Bobić; Maroje Sorić
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Used machine learning with sex, age, BMI, body fat, physical activity, training hours, socioeconomic status and total Functional Movement Screen score to predict one-year injury in nonathletic (n = 364) and athletic (n = 192) 16-17-year-olds from the CRO-PALS cohort. The FMS cut-off (>12) alone gave AUCs of 0.54 and 0.56, ML models did slightly better (best AUC 0.58 Naive Bayes and 0.62 logistic regression), and the authors do not support FMS as an injury prediction tool.
why_useful: Informs indicator selection and the injury-risk prediction module by showing that FMS adds little predictive value and that ML gains over simple cut-offs can be small.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Minimum sample size for external validation of a clinical prediction model with a binary outcome
authors: Richard D. Riley; Thomas P. A. Debray; Gary S. Collins; Lucinda Archer; Joie Ensor; Maarten van Smeden; Kym I. E. Snell
what_it_does: Proposes closed-form and iterative calculations of the minimum sample size for externally validating a binary-outcome prediction model, aiming for precise calibration (O/E and slope), discrimination (C-statistic) and net benefit at decision thresholds. In a worked example with a 1.8% event rate, at least 9835 participants (177 events) were needed to estimate calibration and discrimination precisely, driven by the calibration-slope criterion.
why_useful: Tells the program how many new pilots or cadets it needs to externally validate a binary-outcome prediction model (for example a type-based suitability model) before it supports decisions; the worked example shows rare outcomes need very large samples.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Calculating the sample size required for developing a clinical prediction model
authors: Richard D Riley; Joie Ensor; Kym I E Snell; Frank E Harrell; Glen P Martin; Johannes B Reitsma; Karel G M Moons; Gary Collins; Maarten van Smeden
what_it_does: A guidance article on how to calculate the sample size required to develop a clinical prediction model. It notes that many published models are developed on datasets with too few participants or outcome events, leading to inaccurate predictions and incorrect decisions for some individuals.
why_useful: Gives a way to work out the minimum dataset needed before developing a model that predicts suitability or outcomes from strength and fitness indicators.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Fitness assessments as predictors of performance in police occupational tasks
authors: Elisa F. D. Canetti; Rob Marc Orr; Ben L. Schram; Brown, W; Jay J Dawes
cautions: conference paper, no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Retrospective cohort of 106 law enforcement officers in which multiple regression tested whether five fitness assessments (vertical jump, hand grip strength, leg-back dynamometer, 1-minute push-ups and sit-ups) predicted three occupational tasks. Combined models predicted fence jump (adjusted R2=0.61), 102.3-kg victim drag (0.45) and get-up (0.72); vertical jump contributed to all three, grip strength uniquely added 3% to victim drag and sit-ups 8% to get-up.
why_useful: Informs indicator selection: shows which strength, power and endurance tests carry unique predictive weight for occupational tasks in a tactical population. This way of validating tests against job tasks could carry over to pilot task demands. The R2 values are in-sample and come from a conference abstract.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Current Approaches to the Use of Artificial Intelligence for Injury Risk Assessment and Performance Prediction in Team Sports: a Systematic Review
authors: João Gustavo Claudino; Daniel de Oliveira Capanema; Thiago Vieira de Souza; Julio Cerca Serrão; Adriano C. Machado Pereira; George P. Nassis
what_it_does: Systematic review of 58 studies (pooled 6456 participants, 76% professional athletes) applying 11 AI techniques to injury risk and performance prediction across 12 team sports. Artificial neural networks, decision tree classifiers, support vector machines and Markov processes were used most and reported good performance metrics, and the authors call for prospective evaluation of predictive performance.
why_useful: Informs the choice of prediction-model families and the validation agenda for the program's AI component.

section: AI-based and composite fitness evaluation
title: Helicopter Simulator Performance Prediction Using the Random Forest Method
authors: Hans Bauer; Dennis Nowak; Britta Herbig
full_text_version: the article as reprinted in the author's thesis
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Used Random Forests with conditional permutation variable importance to screen 54 pilot-related and occupational candidate predictors (from self-report questionnaires and aeromedical examination records) of simulator flight performance in two malfunction scenarios, in 51 male European helicopter emergency medical services pilots. Five predictors passed the selection threshold: higher perceived rewards and predictability at work went with better performance, higher physiological dysregulation and alanine aminotransferase went with worse performance, and scores also differed between the two simulator sites.
why_useful: Informs the indicator-selection step of the AI model by showing Random Forest variable-importance screening of many aeromedical and occupational predictors in a small pilot sample, although the outcome is flight performance rather than physical fitness.

title: Jump Assessments on Force Plates Do Not Determine Musculoskeletal Injury Risk in Active-Duty Air Force Personnel
authors: Justin J. Merrigan; Nicole Ray; Kristyn Barrett; Maegan O'Connor; Roger Smith; James R. Walters; Josh Hagen; Jason Eckerle; Robert Briggs

what_it_does: In 963 active-duty Air Force personnel followed for 6 months (88 with lower-extremity musculoskeletal injury), force-plate jump tests were related to injury using logistic regression and percentile-based risk ratios. Higher jump heights were linked to lower injury odds (OR 0.49-0.60), and scores below the 25th percentile carried higher risk ratios than scores above the 75th (2.38-3.53), but no model accurately classified injury occurrence.
why_useful: Informs the injury-risk and decision-support components. In Air Force personnel (not specifically aircrew), force-plate jump metrics alone did not classify injury risk. Scores below the 25th percentile carried higher risk and may flag who needs preparatory training.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: A meta-analytic predictive approach to fitness-related dropout rates of special operations forces candidates
authors: Alain Dössegger; Thomas Gsponer; Christian Protte; Thomas Wyss; Rahel Gilgen-Ammann; Denis Bron; Marina Veil; Martin Flück; Markus Gerber; Zeno Stanga
what_it_does: In a prospective observational study, 137 male special operations forces candidates from the Swiss Armed Forces and police received individualized training recommendations after a fitness assessment. Fitness-related dropout was tracked through selection and compared with historical controls using a Bayesian meta-analytic predictive approach: it was 29% (40 of 137) against a historical average of 42%, with a 91.6% posterior probability of a reduced dropout rate.
why_useful: Informs the decision-support component with evidence from a tactical population: turning fitness assessment results into individualized training recommendations went with lower fitness-related attrition during selection. The design is observational against historical controls, and the abstract does not say how the recommendations were generated.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Aeromedical decision-making for asymptomatic cerebral cavernous malformations in military pilots
authors: Hui Zhang; Li Ma; Cheng-Ye Zhang; Jian Zhou; Yan Zhou; Yu-Dong Ma
what_it_does: Retrospective study of 22 military pilots with 23 asymptomatic cerebral cavernous malformations, in which a multidisciplinary review board judged the risk of in-flight incapacitation (epilepsy and haemorrhage) from established clinical risk factors to decide flight status. Eleven pilots with cortical, brainstem, eloquent-area or Zabramski Type II lesions were permanently disqualified, while 11 with solitary non-cortical, non-eloquent Type III or IV lesions were cleared for unrestricted flying and showed stable lesions and no neurological events over a mean 34-month follow-up, supporting a preliminary risk-stratified certification protocol.
why_useful: A worked example of a tiered fitness-for-duty decision protocol for military pilots (disqualify, or clear with annual monitoring). It can serve as a template for the program's fitness-for-duty recommendations, although its predictors are neurological rather than physical.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Early identification of dropouts during the special forces selection program
authors: Ruud J. R. den Hartigh; Rik Huijzer; Frank J. Blaauw; Age de Wit; Peter de Jonge
what_it_does: Weekly assessments of 249 special forces recruits during selection (self-efficacy, motivation, psychological and physical stress, recovery) were used to build linear regression and machine-learning models predicting dropout. Under cross-validation, linear regression performed relatively well (AUC 0.69) while staying interpretable; low self-efficacy and motivation were the significant predictors, and dropout could often be predicted multiple weeks in advance.
why_useful: Informs decision-support design for selection. It is a cross-validated, interpretable early-warning model built on repeated weekly measures, and it shows the trade-off between accuracy and interpretability along with AUC reporting.

why_useful: Gives a checklist for appraising the quality, risk of bias and applicability of the program's prediction and classification models at both the development and evaluation stages. It was written for healthcare models, so using it on fitness models is an adaptation.

title: Determining cut-off scores for simulated tasks in Brazilian Air Force military personnel
authors: Willian Carrero Botta; J M Magraner; R M Orr; C R Padovani; J P Borin
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request

The agreed standards were obstacle course 3:21, foot march 31:00, plane crash on land 1:25, plane crash on water 1:12 and water survival skills 4:03 (min:s), for monitoring operational capability and guiding conditioning of personnel below standard.
why_useful: Gives a concrete percentile-plus-expert-review procedure for setting pass/fail standards in an air force population, informing how the program turns test results into readiness cut-offs and conditioning recommendations.

why_useful: Sets the reporting standard the program should follow when developing, validating and publishing its fitness-prediction and classification models.

Age, fighter type and C2-7 absolute rotation angle were significant determinants; flying hours, body height and BMI were not.
why_useful: Summarises which predictors held up in the thin multivariable evidence on pilot cervical outcomes, including aircraft (fighter) type, for the injury-risk part of decision support. None of the determinants it pulls together is a strength or fitness measure.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Predictions of attrition among US Marine Corps: Comparison of four predictive methods
authors: Juan Manuel Alzate Vanegas; William Wine; Fritz Drasgow
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser
cautions: no held-out or external validation reported
what_it_does: Compared logistic regression with machine-learning classification models (classification trees and random forests) for predicting training attrition from the US Marine Corps Delayed Enlistment Program using Tailored Adaptive Personality Assessment System (TAPAS) scores, judging performance by type of misclassification error and across reasons for attrition. The low attrition base rate impeded model training, but the machine-learning models outperformed logistic regression in predicting voluntary attrition in a stratified 50% attrition sample.
why_useful: Informs decision-support design for selection. It compares ML with logistic regression on a military attrition outcome with a low base rate and frames performance by misclassification type. The predictors are personality scores, not fitness, and the abstract gives no performance figures.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Musculoskeletal disorders and their associations with health- and work-related factors: a cross-sectional comparison between Swedish air force personnel and army soldiers
authors: Matthias Tegern; Ulrika Aasa; Björn O. Äng; Helena Larsson
what_it_does: Cross-sectional questionnaire study comparing musculoskeletal disorders in 166 male Swedish Air Force personnel (fighter pilots, helicopter pilots, rear crew) and 185 deployed army soldiers. Air Force personnel had higher prevalence of upper-quarter and lumbar disorders, with no difference between the aircrew groups; self-rated physical health below excellent was associated with disorders in both regions, and older age and greater height with lumbar disorders.
why_useful: Gives musculoskeletal-disorder prevalence and associated factors (self-rated health, age, height) in fighter pilots, helicopter pilots and rear crew, and supports adding MSD questions and screening for air force personnel, informing the injury-risk input to fitness-for-duty decisions; the study is questionnaire-only, with no strength or fitness measures.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Association Between Musculoskeletal Injuries and the Canadian Armed Forces Physical Employment Standard Proxy in Canadian Military Recruits
authors: Etienne Chassé; Marie-Andrée Laroche; Carole-Anne Dufour; Renaud Guimond; François Lalonde
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Using records of Canadian recruits in Basic Military Qualification in 2016-2017, t-tests and stepwise logistic regression related age, sex, waist circumference, predicted VO2peak and FORCE test scores (20 m rushes, sandbag lift, intermittent loaded shuttles, sandbag drag) to musculoskeletal injuries that needed the Training Rehabilitation Program (rate 4.3%). Recruits more than 1 SD below the mean on rushes, loaded shuttles or sandbag drag were 2.26-2.74 times more likely to sustain such an injury (2.19 times for low VO2peak), and sex, age and waist circumference had no effect once FORCE performance was controlled for.
why_useful: Shows how job-related fitness test results with below-norm cut-offs can feed injury-risk screening, informing the fitness-for-duty and injury-risk side of decision support.

title: A framework for the design and development of physical employment tests and standards
authors: W. Payne; J. Harvey

what_it_does: Presents a framework for designing physical employment tests and standards for uniformed services (military, police, fire and emergency), comparing generic predictive, task-related predictive and task-simulation testing. It covers choosing tests through job task analysis, physical demands analysis and correlation analysis, judging them on measurability, discriminating power, reliability, validity and practicality, and setting standards by criterion or norm referencing.
why_useful: Informs how the program chooses its strength and fitness test battery, checks each test's reliability and validity, and sets criterion- or norm-referenced cut-offs for selection and assignment decisions.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: 飞行人员感音神经性聋特许飞行医学鉴定指南
authors: 全军航空航天医学专业委员会; 金占国
venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Guideline from the Chinese military aerospace medicine committee for waiver (special-permission) aeromedical assessment of aircrew with sensorineural hearing loss, for which current aircrew medical standards have no specific waiver clause. It notes that such waivers are now decided by weighing aircraft type, flight duties, unit needs and the aviator's wish to keep flying, without quantitative criteria, and was drawn up by committee experts, drawing on national military-standard research, to give a scientific, standardized and unified basis for these assessments.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning in sports medicine: mapping clinical tasks and assessing clinical maturity - a scoping review
authors: Jakob Lindskog; Kristian Heder Ternell; Yinan Yu; Ida Lindman; Kristian Samuelsson; Eric Hamrin Senorski
venue: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
what_it_does: Scoping review of 97 studies (from 8,677 records in MEDLINE, EMBASE and Web of Science) on AI and ML applied in sports medicine. Most covered orthopaedics (70.1%) and neurology (18.6%), and predictive and estimation models were the main application (57.7%). Reported discrimination was often high, but most studies used retrospective data and internal validation, calibration was rarely reported and prospective workflow integration was rare, so the authors treat these tools as supportive adjuncts rather than autonomous decision-makers.
why_useful: Informs the program's validation and deployment standards by naming the gaps an AI fitness or injury-risk model should close (internal-only validation, missing calibration, no prospective integration) and by framing such tools as decision adjuncts.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: AI-enabled instructor care and physical fitness performance in police cadets: the mediating roles of emotions, engagement, and recovery
authors: Zeyu Zhang; Mahpiret Kanji; Xiaomei Lu
what_it_does: Quasi-experimental pre-post study of 224 police cadets in four classes. Two classes (n=112) used an AI-enabled dashboard that generated weekly care signals from training and self-report indicators and prompted instructors to give standardized supportive actions, including individualized training suggestions; the other two (n=112) trained as usual. Difference-in-differences models showed a net gain in physical fitness performance (0-100 scale; beta=3.48, p<0.001), with exploratory mediation through emotions, engagement, sleep quality and burnout.
why_useful: Informs the decision-support delivery layer by showing a human-in-the-loop design in which AI-generated signals prompt instructor training actions, evaluated against fitness outcomes in a tactical cohort.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Selecting force plate tests and metrics to complement physical preparation strategies prior to commencing strenuous military training courses
authors: Peter Ladlow; Nicholas J. Ripley; Damjana V. Cabarkapa; Dimitrije Cabarkapa; Dale W. Chapman; Mary Claire Geneau; G. Gregory Haff; Lachlan P. James; Paul Jones; Jason P. Lake; Christopher J. Sole; Anthony Turner; Marina De Vecchis; Natalie Masters; Charles Coussens; Robyn Holton; Russell J. Coppack; Colin Suffield; Paul Comfort
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
what_it_does: Online survey of 10 experienced force plate users to agree which force plate tests and metrics should be added to a pre-course physical performance battery that assesses physical readiness, musculoskeletal injury risk and likelihood of passing an arduous military training course. Consensus was strong for multi-joint isometric tests, countermovement jump and drop jump but not for metrics; the metrics were then judged on biomechanical relevance, redundancy, reliability, test duration, interpretability and feasibility to agree a minimum test and metric dataset.
why_useful: Informs the choice of force-plate strength and power indicators for pre-training readiness screening, a building block for strength-based typing and training-track suitability decisions.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Importance of strength training to prevent secondary lower limb musculoskeletal injury in military personnel
authors: Peter Ladlow; Russell J Coppack; Robyn P Cassidy; Rachel Rodgers; Robert Barker-Davies; Paul Comfort; Nicholas J Ripley; Christopher Bramah; Colin Suffield; Debra Hayhurst; Marina De Vecchis; Samual R Higgins; Alexander N Bennett; Oliver O’Sullivan
what_it_does: Narrative review arguing that maximal force and rapid force (rate of force development, reactive strength) should be trained and assessed in late-stage rehabilitation of military personnel after lower-limb musculoskeletal injury, noting that low strength and prior injury are linked to higher injury risk. It discusses how strength assessment should inform return-to-duty exit criteria and physical employment standards.
why_useful: Informs strength indicator selection (maximal force, rate of force development, reactive strength) and the design of strength-based return-to-duty or fitness-for-duty thresholds in military personnel.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Development of two physical employment standard tests for aviation rescue firefighters with different ecological validity
authors: Tim LA Doyle; Jodie A Wills; Rhiannon A Campbell; Brendan Parsey
venue: WORK: A Journal of Prevention, Assessment & Rehabilitation
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Develops physical employment standard tests for incumbent aviation rescue firefighters from trade-task workshops, field observations and a confirmation workshop, comparing an operational-equipment test with a hybrid operational-plus-gym test (Phase 1 n = 20, Phase 2 n = 42). Distance travelled and RPE were close to live scenarios, though reported intensity was much lower in scenarios (24.9 vs about 65-67 m/min); oxygen-consumption and heart-rate data were presented as supporting physiological equivalence, and the hybrid test with time-based segment standards was recommended.
why_useful: Shows a defensible task-analysis-to-test-to-time-standard workflow that could be adapted to set role- or aircraft-specific physical standards for suitability and fitness-for-duty decisions.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Assessing Ergonomic Risk Loads on Pilots Across Diverse Aircraft Types: Uçak Tiplerinin Pilotlar Üzerinde Oluşturduğu Ergonomik Risk Yükleri
authors: Ibrahim Talha Ucar; Selçuk Çebi
what_it_does: Applies the Quick Exposure Check ergonomic method to pilots of different aircraft types to assess exposure to work-related musculoskeletal disorder risk factors; no sample size is given in the abstract. It reports that ergonomic risk burden may differ by aircraft type and identifies the back, shoulder/arm, wrist/hand and neck as the body regions at risk.
why_useful: Informs aircraft-type-specific indicator selection: points to the body regions (back, shoulder/arm, wrist/hand, neck) where strength measures may matter most when judging suitability for an aircraft type.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: The Use of Force Plate Technology to Measure Force Production Characteristics in Military Personnel: A Scoping Review of Methodological Reporting Practices
authors: Peter Ladlow; Kieran M. Lunt; Paul Comfort; Oliver O’Sullivan; Francisco J Robles-Palazón; Nicholas J. Ripley; John J. McMahon; Natalie Masters; Robyn P. Cassidy; Marina De Vecchis; Vanessa Bell; Alexander N. Bennett; Russell J. Coppack
what_it_does: Scoping review of 40 studies using force plates to measure maximal and rapid lower-limb force production in military personnel for occupational task performance, injury-risk profiling and rehabilitation. It found major inconsistencies in reporting of test preparation, execution and analysis: the IMTP and CMJ were the most used tests, researchers commonly reported no more than two, mainly outcome-based, metrics per test, and most IMTP studies used incorrect coaching instructions or none.
why_useful: Informs strength-measurement standardisation and indicator selection: lists the protocol and reporting details (surface, zeroing, weighing, cueing, footwear, filters, thresholds, metric phase) a program using IMTP and CMJ force-plate indicators needs to fix and report.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Explainable artificial intelligence for gait analysis: advances, pitfalls, and challenges - a systematic review
authors: Liangliang Xiang; Zixiang Gao; Peimin Yu; Justin Fernandez; Yaodong Gu; Ruoli Wang; Elena M. Gutierrez-Farewik
what_it_does: PROSPERO-registered systematic review of 31 studies (from 3,676 records) applying explainable AI to gait analysis, grouped into model-agnostic (16), model-specific (12) and hybrid (3) approaches, mostly local methods such as SHAP and LIME, in populations such as Parkinson's disease, stroke, sarcopenia and cerebral palsy. Biomechanically meaningful features such as stride length and joint angles emerged as key discriminators, while standardisation, validation and balancing accuracy against transparency remain open problems.
why_useful: Informs the explainability layer of the decision-support design: which explanation methods suit movement data and which validation and standardisation gaps to address.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Isokinetic Shoulder Strength and its Associations to Injury in Tactical Populations: A Critical Review
authors: Michael S Wilkinson; Joshua H. Guy; Steven J. Obst
what_it_does: Critical review of 19 studies (17 military, 2 firefighter) that used isokinetic shoulder testing in tactical populations, six of which examined injury. Concentric internal/external rotation at 60 degrees/s was used in most cases, protocols were narrow, and a best-evidence synthesis found conflicting evidence that isokinetic shoulder strength is associated with injury.
why_useful: Guides the choice of isokinetic shoulder-strength protocol and warns against treating shoulder strength alone as an injury-risk indicator.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Characterising the physical demands of critical tasks across the Royal Australian Air Force
authors: Greg L. Carstairs; Scott W. Michael; Herbert Groeller; Jace R. Drain
venue: WORK: A Journal of Prevention, Assessment & Rehabilitation
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Job task analysis of 27 RAAF trades identified 87 criterion tasks, 92% manual-handling dominant, with muscular strength a principal capacity in 59% (muscular endurance 52%, cardiorespiratory endurance 39%) and Lift to Platform (44%) and Lift and Carry (38%) the most common movement clusters. Lift-to-platform tasks had a median height of 1.32 m and median mass of 25.0 kg per person, and the authors conclude current fitness assessments are unlikely to predict job task performance.
why_useful: Shows that strength-dominant manual handling characterises critical tasks across RAAF trades (aircrew not specified) and that generic fitness tests may not predict task performance; its job-task-analysis and movement-cluster approach could be adapted to define role-specific strength demands for pilots.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Association between physical fitness and musculoskeletal health in firefighters
authors: Jaron Ras; Elpidoforos S. Soteriades; Denise L. Smith; Andre P. Kengne; Lloyd Leach
what_it_does: Cross-sectional study of 308 full-time Cape Town firefighters relating fitness tests (non-exercise estimated VO2max, grip and leg strength, push-ups, sit-ups, sit-and-reach) to self-reported musculoskeletal injury and discomfort. Higher estimated VO2max, push-ups, sit-ups and sit-and-reach were linked to lower odds of injury, while higher push-up and sit-up capacity were linked to higher odds of discomfort at several body sites.
why_useful: Evidence from a tactical population on which fitness and strength-endurance tests relate to musculoskeletal injury, useful when choosing injury-risk indicators.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Impact of a 5-Week Individualised Training Program on Physical Performance and Measures Associated with Musculoskeletal Injury Risk in Army Personnel: A Pilot Study
authors: Chelsea Smith; Kenji Doma; Brian Heilbronn; Anthony Leicht
what_it_does: Small randomised 'pilot' trial (not aviation): 19 Australian Army soldiers were allocated to 5 weeks of individualised, force-plate-guided training or standard group training (results reported for 8 vs 9) and tested on push-ups, a multistage fitness test, 3RM lifts, loaded march time and technology-based jump, balance and plank tests. The individualised group improved loaded march time significantly less than controls (-0.7% vs -5.1%, p = 0.03) and deadlift 3RM more, but not significantly (20.6% vs 8.4%, p = 0.056); other outcomes were similar, and the authors concluded the approach was feasible and mostly comparable to standard training.
why_useful: Informs the training-recommendation side of decision support with a military field trial of turning force-plate and strength assessments into individualised programs, which proved feasible but showed no clear advantage.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Designing criterion measures for physically demanding jobs
authors: Deborah L. Gebhardt; Todd A. Baker
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser
what_it_does: Overviews the types of criterion measures used to assess the physical domain of physically demanding civilian and military jobs and approaches for designing and evaluating them. It also presents a method for generating criterion measures that apply across multiple jobs.
why_useful: Informs validation design: how to define job-related criterion measures for validating physical-test cut-offs or physical-type assignments for role suitability.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Test-retest reliability of isometric mid-thigh pull maximum strength assessment: a systematic review
authors: Jozo Grgic; Bela Scapec; Pavle Mikulic; Zeljko Pedisic
what_it_does: A systematic review of 16 good-to-excellent quality studies (rated with COSMIN) on the test-retest reliability of isometric mid-thigh pull peak force. Median ICC was 0.96 and median CV 4.9%, with good-to-excellent reliability for absolute and relative peak force and for bilateral and unilateral tests.
why_useful: Reference reliability values for a whole-body isometric strength measure that could be part of pilot strength profiling.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: A Critical Review of the Baseline Soldier Physical Readiness Requirements Study
authors: Kyle A. Novak
what_it_does: Critically re-examines the model behind the US Army's Baseline Soldier Physical Readiness Requirements Study, which moved the Army fitness test of record from gender- and age-specific to gender- and age-neutral task-based standards and produced the six-event Army Combat Fitness Test. It reports critical mistakes in the model and a lack of rigorous cross-validation.
why_useful: Informs validation standards and indicator selection: a cautionary example of a military fitness-test event-selection model criticised for modelling errors and missing cross-validation.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Artificial Intelligence in Pilot Training and Education – Towards a Machine Learning Aided Instructor Assistant for Flight Simulators
authors: Shuiqiao Yang; Kun Yu; Thorsten Lammers; Fang Chen
venue: Communications in Computer and Information Science
cautions: abstract unavailable, summarised from the title, conference paper
what_it_does: Abstract unavailable; by title, describes work toward a machine-learning-aided instructor assistant for flight-simulator pilot training.
why_useful: A possible example for designing decision support in pilot training (an ML aid for instructor judgments); the full text is needed to confirm it has a real model and evaluation.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Use of body composition characteristics in developing a screening model for general physical fitness of police officers
authors: Filip Kukić
venue: National Repository of Dissertations in Serbia
what_it_does: Doctoral dissertation relating multifrequency bioelectrical-impedance body composition indices to physical fitness in 199 male police officers, 45 women (19 officers, 26 cadets) and 196 male police cadets, to test their predictive power and build a fitness screening model. The truncated abstract gives no results.
why_useful: Informs the screening and prediction component by showing how body-composition indices can be turned into a fitness screening model in a tactical population.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: A development framework for decision support systems in high-performance sport
authors: Xavier Schelling; Sam Robertson
venue: International Journal of Computer Science in Sport
what_it_does: Conceptual paper that draws on the literature to propose a framework for developing and evaluating decision support systems in high-performance sport. It sets three criteria (context satisfaction, output quality, process efficiency) resting on six components: feasibility, delivered knowledge, decisional guidance, data quality, system error and system complexity.
why_useful: Informs decision-support design and evaluation: a structured set of criteria (feasibility, data quality, system error, decisional guidance) for building and auditing the program's recommendation module.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Inter-rater and test-retest reliability of movement control tests for the neck, shoulder, thoracic, lumbar, and hip regions in military personnel
authors: Matthias Tegern; Ulrika Aasa; Björn O. Äng; Karin Harms-Ringdahl; Helena Larsson
what_it_does: Assessed inter-rater (n = 37) and test-retest (n = 45) reliability of 15 movement control tests for the neck, shoulder, thoracic, lumbar and hip regions in Swedish Armed Forces personnel rated by physiotherapists. Inter-rater kappa ranged from .19 to .95 (seven tests above .60) and test-retest kappa from .26 to .65, and a subset of tests was judged reliable for screening military aviators.
why_useful: Identifies which movement-control tests are reliable enough to add to an aviator musculoskeletal-injury screening component alongside strength indicators.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: +Gz Exposure and Spinal Injury-Induced Flight Duty Limitations
authors: Tuomas Honkanen; Roope Sovelius; Matti Mäntysaari; Heikki Kyröläinen; Janne Avela; Tuomo K. Leino
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Compared Finnish Air Force pilots flying with +Gz limitations due to spinal disorders (n=23) against 50 symptomless controls with over 1000 flight hours on sortie-by-sortie cumulative +Gz exposure (fatigue index) and flight hours over the first 5 career years. Neither early-career cumulative +Gz exposure nor flight hours was associated with spinal flight duty limitation (mean fatigue index 8.0 vs 7.7).
why_useful: Background for an injury-risk or fitness-for-duty component: it defines spinal flight duty limitation as an outcome in military pilots and shows that early-career cumulative Gz exposure alone did not predict it. It has no fitness or strength measures and no predictive model.
notes: Summarised in Honkanen's 2019 doctoral thesis, which is in this list with its PDF; the online thesis does not reprint this article.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Reliability and agreement of the IsoKai isokinetic lift test – A test used for admission to the Swedish Armed Forces
authors: Tony Bohman; Matthias Tegern; Alexandra Halvarsson; Lisbet Broman; Helena Larsson
what_it_does: The IsoKai isokinetic lift test used for Swedish Armed Forces admission was tested in male conscripts (intrarater n = 534, interrater n = 137) over two sessions about two hours apart. ICCs were excellent (interrater 0.942 for mean force, 0.858 for peak force), SEM and smallest real difference were reported, and Bland-Altman analysis showed no systematic error.
why_useful: A large-sample example of reporting reliability and smallest real difference for a maximal dynamic strength test already used in military admission, which the authors suggest for selection and for tracking strength change.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: A contribution to the methodological framework of establishing cardiorespiratory-based physical employment standards
authors: Adam Hayes
full_text: Free online; the site blocks automated downloads, so open the link in a browser
what_it_does: A thesis that investigated the critical steps of a methodological framework for establishing a bona fide cardiorespiratory-based physical employment standard: developing task simulations, determining a minimum performance standard, and validating cardiorespiratory-based tests. It responds to doubts about how accurately such tests separate physically capable from incapable employees, and to inconsistent methods for setting minimum standards.
why_useful: Informs threshold setting and validation with a stepwise framework (task simulation, minimum standard, test validation) for bona fide fitness standards, though it covers aerobic rather than strength measures.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Red, Amber, or Green? Athlete Monitoring in Team Sport: The Need for Decision-Support Systems
authors: Samuel Robertson; Jonathan D. Bartlett; Paul B. Gastin
venue: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
what_it_does: Practitioner-oriented paper on traffic-light (red/amber/green) decision-support systems used in team sport to flag athlete performance status or training availability, noting the lack of standardization in how they are run. It discusses data types and formats, analysis approaches, and how to visualize and communicate results to stakeholders, with recommendations for future systems.
why_useful: Informs decision-support design and reporting: how to turn fitness monitoring results into colour-coded status flags and present them to decision-makers.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Predictors of Military Task Performance: Maximal Lift Capacity
authors: Jay R. Hydren; Alexander S. Borges; Marilyn A. Sharp
venue: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 reports in military personnel correlating predictor tests with maximal lift capacity, with predictors grouped into 10 fitness domains. Lean body mass was the strongest overall predictor (alone accounting for about 69% of variance), dynamic strength tests correlated more strongly than strength-endurance tests, and six domains had pooled correlations of 0.40 or greater in combined-sex samples.
why_useful: Ranks which strength and body-composition measures best predict maximal lift capacity in military personnel, evidence that can guide the choice of strength indicators, although the criterion is a lifting task rather than a flight task.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Why screening tests to predict injury do not work—and probably never will…: a critical review
authors: Roald Bahr
what_it_does: Critical review arguing that validating a screening test to predict and prevent sports injury takes three steps: a strong prospective association between the test marker and injury, adequate test properties in relevant populations using appropriate statistics, and evidence that targeting screened high-risk athletes beats giving the same intervention to everyone. It concludes that no current sports-injury screening test has adequate test properties and no intervention study supports screening for injury risk.
why_useful: Informs validation standards for any injury-risk or fitness-for-duty prediction, warning that a significant association does not give accurate individual prediction and that screening must outperform universal intervention.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Prevalence of Neck and Back Pain amongst Aircrew at the Extremes of Anthropometric Measurements
authors: Patricia L. Walters; James M. Cox; Kareem Clayborne; Alyssa J. Hathaway
what_it_does: Measured nine anthropometric parameters and surveyed 88 aviators, in a helicopter-aircrew context, about flying-related neck and back pain. 82% reported flying-related back pain and 58% neck pain; no single anthropometric measure predicted postural complaints, while smaller sitting height, fewer flying hours and heavier NVG counterbalance weight were associated with less neck pain.
why_useful: Informs whether anthropometric variables such as sitting height should sit alongside strength indicators in aircrew injury-risk screening.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Physiological employment standards I. Occupational fitness standards: objectively subjective?
authors: M. J. Tipton; G. S. Milligan; T. J. Reilly
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Examines how a minimum occupational fitness standard is set (choosing the critical task, defining minimum acceptable performance and best-practice execution, determining physical demands and a reasonable relative workload, producing the final standard) and where subjective decisions enter alongside objective measurement. It concludes that all standards involve some subjectivity and recommends documenting the rationale, methods and evidence behind those decisions as an audit trail that supports defensibility.
why_useful: Guides how the program sets and documents the cut-offs behind its selection and fitness-for-duty recommendations so they remain defensible.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Allometric scaling of strength measurements to body size
authors: J. P. Folland; T. M. Mc Cauley; A. G. Williams
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Knee-extensor isometric force and torque at four velocities (0-4.19 rad/s) were measured in 86 young men and scaled to body mass, height and fat-free mass; fat-free mass explained 31% of force and 52-58% of torque variance, and absolute strength and even body-mass-normalised torque were influenced by height, whereas fat-free-mass-normalised strength was not. Fat-free mass is the recommended scaling variable (exponents 0.76 for force, 1.12 for torque), with lower body-mass exponents (0.45 force, 0.68 torque) for relatively homogeneous lean groups.
why_useful: Gives measured scaling exponents and the case for scaling by fat-free mass, which helps decide how to normalise pilot strength scores; the sample was young men only.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Neck pain and related disability in helicopter pilots: A survey of prevalence and risk factors.
authors: Björn Olov Äng; Karin Harms‐Ringdahl
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: 127 Swedish helicopter pilots completed a structured questionnaire on flight-related and individual risk indicators and neck pain, and multivariate regressions estimated relative risks. 3-month prevalence was 57%; previous neck pain and recent shoulder pain were significant risk factors, while strength training showed a non-significant trend toward lower risk.
why_useful: Prevalence and multivariate risk-factor estimates for neck pain in helicopter pilots, including the link between frequent pain and interference with flying duty. These are candidate inputs for an injury-risk or fitness-for-duty component. Strength itself was not measured, and self-reported strength training showed only a non-significant trend.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Quantifying Test-Retest Reliability Using the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient and the SEM
authors: Joseph P. Weir
venue: The Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: A review of how to choose and interpret ICC forms, depending on whether systematic error is included in the denominator, and how to calculate the SEM from them. It shows how the SEM gives confidence intervals for individual scores and the minimal difference needed to be confident that an individual's change is real.
why_useful: Supplies the SEM and minimal-difference formulas needed to judge whether a pilot's score change, or a move across a type boundary, is real.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: 飞行员医学失能风险的评估与管理策略——1％法则的建立与发展
authors: 周毓瑾
venue: 中华航空航天医学杂志
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Reviews the EU-promoted 1% rule for pilot medical incapacitation (16 papers, reviews, reports and standards plus 1 monograph), covering incapacitation risk-assessment methods, risk evaluation models and risk control and management strategies. Concludes that aeromedical certification should centre on a pilot's absolute incapacitation risk rather than disease-specific attributable risk, providing criteria for setting standards and making certification decisions.
why_useful: Decision-support design: an absolute-risk threshold logic for turning assessed risk into fit/unfit certification decisions, adaptable to mapping fitness results onto duty recommendations.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Muscle Strength Testing
authors: Slobodan Jaric
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: A review arguing that strength results are often not normalised for body size, or are normalised inappropriately or inconsistently, which confounds athletic profiles and functional-performance assessments and prevents comparison across studies. It recommends routine use of an allometric, body-mass-based strength index with exponent b = 0.67 for dynamometer force and b = 1 for isokinetic torque, and body-size-independent indices of movement performance as well.
why_useful: Gives recommended allometric exponents for normalising strength indicators to body mass before scoring or typing pilots of different body sizes.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Measures of Reliability in Sports Medicine and Science
authors: Will G. Hopkins
what_it_does: A review of reliability measures: within-subject variation (the typical error, often as a CV), systematic change in the mean, and retest correlation, with limits of agreement described as a biased, more limited measure. It recommends about 50 participants and at least 3 trials for reasonable precision and lists uses including decisions when monitoring individuals.
why_useful: The standard sport-science framework for measuring error in each strength indicator, which limits how confidently individuals can be placed in types.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: Incorporating occupational medicine methodology into military fitness for duty and readiness issues.
authors: Stephen E. Popper
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Narrative review arguing that the U.S. Air Force's limited fitness-for-duty and readiness programme should adopt occupational medicine methods (determining job requirements, assessing individuals, monitoring performance over time) together with current physical-performance knowledge. It recommends job-specific and entry physical fitness standards with ongoing testing, evaluation and training, ending the weight-management and cycle-ergometry programmes, treating body fat only as a medical condition, and case-management teams for injured or underperforming personnel.
why_useful: For the decision-support layer, gives a military occupational-medicine rationale for job-specific fitness standards and a structured process for fitness-for-duty, return-to-duty and case management.

section: Decision support, explainability and validation standards
title: The New Air Force Fitness Test: A Field Trial Assessing Effectiveness and Safety
authors: John R. Sharp
full_text: No free copy found; needs a subscription or a library request
what_it_does: Field trial in which 2,139 U.S. Air Force members were sorted into risk categories by a questionnaire on exercise habits and risk factors. At-risk members were interviewed by a practitioner and placed in a supervised fitness programme or exempted, and all others took the 1.5-mile run. From these data the authors estimated that 50% of the force would pass the old category III standard and 33% the new category IV standard, and that only 7.9% would be exempted after interview (almost all for cardiac conditions), with little added workload for medical facilities.
why_useful: Informs the program's pre-test safety screening and standard-setting steps, with a field-tested questionnaire-plus-interview triage (test, supervise or exempt) and pass rates under the old and new standards.
